title: RetNet retention at nano scale: parallel == recurrent to 3e-7, and the decay schedule is worth 12.7x the seed noise
hypothesis: Hand-rolled multi-scale retention reproduces the RetNet parallel/recurrent duality to floating-point precision (max abs logit deviation <= ~1e-5); on a tiny char LM at matched params/steps retention trails softmax attention in val bits/char; and the decay schedule (multi-scale geometric vs uniform vs no-decay vs learned) makes a difference smaller than seed-to-seed noise.
question: Is the RetNet duality numerically exact at nano scale, does retention actually trail softmax attention on a char LM at matched budget, and does the decay schedule gamma_h matter at all?
method: Hand-rolled multi-scale retention in pure PyTorch (no yet-another-retnet dependency), implemented TWICE: parallel form Y=(Q K^T . D)V with D[n,m]=gamma_h^(n-m) on the causal triangle, and recurrent form S_t = gamma_h S_{t-1} + k_t^T v_t, y_t = q_t S_t, sharing an identical post-path (headwise GroupNorm -> swish gate -> output projection) so any gap is pure float error. Model: 2 pre-norm blocks, d_model 64, 4 heads (d_head 16), d_ff 192, ctx 128, char vocab 65, learned absolute position embeddings, 108,032 params. Reference arm: standard causal softmax MHA, iso-parameter by binary-searching its d_ff to 225 -> 108,098 params (0.061% spread). Four retention arms differ ONLY in gamma: (i) paper multi-scale 1-2^-(5+h) = .96875/.984375/.992188/.996094, (ii) uniform .97, (iii) no decay 1.0 (= pure causal linear attention), (iv) learned sigmoid(theta_h) initialised at the multi-scale values. All 5 arms: tiny-shakespeare char level 90/10 split, 800 steps, batch 16 x ctx 128 (1.64M tokens), AdamW lr 2e-3 (60-step warmup, cosine to 10%), wd 0.1, clip 1.0, IDENTICAL seeded batch stream, 2 seeds. Metric: val bits/char on a fixed 40-batch held-out set. Equivalence measured at T in {16,32,64,128} on both freshly-initialised and trained weights.
architecture: hand-rolled RetNet multi-scale retention (parallel + recurrent forms) vs softmax attention, 2-layer pre-norm char LM, d_model 64, 4 heads, d_ff 192/225, ctx 128, 0.108M params

metrics.headline: parallel vs recurrent max abs logit deviation 3.0e-07 at init / 4.8e-06 trained, FLAT in sequence length (rel dev ~1 float32 epsilon); decay-schedule spread 0.2469 bpc = 12.7x the 0.0195 seed spread, ranking learned 3.150 < uniform-.97 3.271 < attention 3.274 < paper multi-scale 3.298 < no-decay 3.397

result_summary: Two of three hypotheses held; the third was refuted hard. (1) DUALITY CONFIRMED and it is float32-exact: same weights, same batch, parallel vs recurrent max abs logit deviation is 2.4-3.0e-07 at init and 2.4-4.8e-06 after training, with max RELATIVE deviation 1.4-3.4e-07 (~one float32 epsilon) and FLAT in sequence length across T=16/32/64/128 - the recurrence does not drift - identical for all four decay schedules including gamma=1. That beats the ~1e-5 target by 2-40x. Honest aside: on CPU the Python-loop recurrent form is 4.4x SLOWER than the parallel one at B=4,T=128 (28.9 vs 6.5 ms); the recurrent form's win is asymptotic/memory, not wall clock at this size. (2) RETENTION vs ATTENTION is a wash at matched budget: the paper's multi-scale retention trails iso-parameter softmax attention by only +0.0239 bpc (1.2 seed-spreads), and uniform-gamma retention ties it (-0.0032). (3) THE DECAY SCHEDULE IS THE BIG LEVER - the pre-registered null is dead. Spread across the four schedules is 0.2469 bpc = 12.7x the max seed spread (0.0195), every adjacent pair fully seed-separated: learned 3.1496 < uniform .97 3.2706 < attention 3.2738 < paper multi-scale 3.2977 < no-decay (pure causal linear attention) 3.3965. Three sub-findings: (a) removing decay entirely is the worst arm by 0.10 bpc, so the decay is load-bearing not cosmetic; (b) ONE tuned scalar gamma shared by all heads BEATS the paper's geometric multi-scale ladder by 0.027 bpc in both seeds, so multi-scale-ness is not what pays; (c) what pays is the TIMESCALE - a naked sigmoid-parameterised learned gamma (8 extra params total) pulls every head DOWN from its multi-scale init in both layers and both seeds, half-lives 22/44/88/177 chars -> 7.5/16/29/57 chars (seed agreement +-1 char), and wins by 0.124 bpc over attention (6.4 seed-spreads); its lead over uniform GROWS monotonically through training (behind at step 200, -0.121 by step 800), so it is not an early-training artifact. Framed against this lab's zoology rows, both results are one fact from two sides: on MQAR, decay-gated linear attention sits on the query-ignoring guessing floor (2026-07-25_zoology-mqar-recall, 2026-07-26_mqar-state-capacity); here it matches attention on language - and optimisation got there by choosing to FORGET FASTER (7-57 char half-lives inside a 128-char window). The decay that buys bits/char is precisely the decay that destroys recall. Caveats: undertrained (800 steps / 1.64M tokens, all curves still descending, absolute bpc 3.15-3.40), 0.108M params, ctx 128 - short enough that two of the paper's four heads barely decay at all inside the window, which limits how far 'multi-scale loses' generalises - iso-hyperparameter rather than per-arm-tuned LR, no xPos (learned absolute position embeddings shared with the attention arm instead), 2 seeds.

novelty_check.conclusion: The mechanism is fully published, the specific comparison is not. RetNet (2307.08621) defines the parallel/recurrent/chunkwise forms and the gamma_h = 1 - 2^-(5+h) schedule, asserts the duality without publishing a numerical deviation, and its ablation table varies the gate / GroupNorm / architecture - NOT the decay schedule. fkodom/yet-another-retnet ships unit tests asserting parallel/recurrent/chunkwise agreement, so equivalence testing per se is not new; what we add is a measured deviation-vs-sequence-length curve at both freshly-initialised and trained weights. 'Disentangle to Decay' (COLING 2025, 2025.coling-main.660) makes decay factors trainable for linear attention at 137M on OpenWebText and reports gains over fixed and directly-trained decay, but states explicitly that it does NOT compare against RetNet. To our search no published work puts the four schedules - paper multi-scale vs one uniform scalar vs no decay vs learned - head to head under a single matched-everything control (iso-param 0.061%, iso-step, identical batch stream, 2 seeds) with softmax attention as an iso-parameter reference, and none does so at <=1M params on char-level data; the finding that the paper's own schedule loses to a single tuned scalar is, to our search, unreported. arXiv/OpenAlex APIs 403 from this environment (scripts/novelty_check.py returned 'unchecked'); verdict rests on web search plus a direct read of the COLING paper.

title: Nano CTM parity: the synchronization readout wins, but a single-tick pair-product control takes most of the win
hypothesis: On cumulative (prefix) parity, at matched core / internal ticks / parameters / steps, the Continuous Thought Machine's neuron-pair SYNCHRONIZATION readout is not doing the work the paper attributes to it: a last-tick or mean-over-ticks readout on the SAME recurrent core, and a plain GRU with a last-state readout, will land within seed-to-seed noise of it, i.e. the win is recurrence depth (T), not neuron-timing synchronization.
question: Is neuron-timing synchronization the signal in a CTM, or is the sync readout just a proxy for recurrence depth (or for something even cheaper)?
method: Hand-rolled nano CTM in pure PyTorch (no code from SakanaAI/continuous-thought-machines). Shared core for four of five arms: a 12-bit binary string is presented STATICALLY as token+position embeddings; at each of T internal ticks the model forms a query from its own post-activations, attends over the 12 bit-slots, feeds [z_{t-1}, o_t] through a synapse MLP to pre-activations a_t, keeps a rolling window of the last M=4 pre-activations per neuron, and passes each neuron's private history through its OWN small MLP (4->8->1, one per neuron, N=64 neurons). ONLY the readout differs, each a single linear projection to 12x2 prefix-parity logits: (a) sync = CTM synchronization matrix, decay-weighted time-average of 256 neuron-pair products over the tick history (numer_t = r*numer_{t-1} + z_i z_j, denom_t = r*denom_{t-1} + 1, S = numer/sqrt(denom), learnable per-pair r); (b) last = last-tick post-activation vector (64-d); (c) mean = mean post-activation over ticks (64-d); (e) pairlast = ADDED CONTROL, the same 256 neuron-pair products evaluated at the LAST TICK ONLY (same quadratic feature, same dimensionality, zero time-integration); (d) gru = plain GRUCell core with last-state readout, no per-neuron history MLPs. Iso-parameter: the sync arm is the reference (55,800 params) and every other arm's free width is integer-searched to match it (last/mean synapse hidden 286 vs sync's 256; GRU hidden 109); realised spread across all 30 runs 0.46%. Loss is the CTM's own two-tick objective (mean of the loss at the min-loss tick and at the max-certainty tick), applied identically to every arm; evaluation reports the paper's max-certainty-tick prediction on a fixed 2000-string held-out set shared by all runs (final-tick numbers also recorded, same ranking). Held fixed: 475 steps, batch 64, AdamW lr 3e-3 (warmup+cosine), wd 0.01, grad-clip 1.0, identical seeded batch stream per seed, identical fixed 256-pair subset. 5 arms x T in {4,16} x 3 seeds = 30 runs. run.py times every (arm,T) cell first and then picks ONE global step count for all 30 runs so no arm is ever silently given more optimisation than another.
architecture: hand-rolled nano Continuous Thought Machine: attention over bit-slots + synapse MLP + 64 per-neuron history MLPs (M=4), 5 swappable readouts, 0.056M params, iso-parameter to 0.46%

dataset.name: synthetic random binary strings, cumulative (prefix) parity
dataset.source: generated in run.py by torch.randint with fixed generator seeds; 2000-string held-out eval set at generator seed 999

task: cumulative/prefix parity of a 12-bit binary string presented statically (12 binary outputs per string); metric = prefix-parity bit accuracy at the max-certainty internal tick, chance 0.5
compute: CPU 1 thread, 652s (10.9 min) for 30 training runs + calibration + evaluations

metrics.headline: at T=16 (bit acc, chance 0.5, 3 seeds): sync 0.674 > pairlast 0.652 > last 0.618 > mean 0.577 > gru 0.568; sync-minus-last +0.056 is seed-separated, but the single-tick pair-product control takes 0.034 of that 0.056 (and ties sync outright at T=4, 0.685 vs 0.687), so the quadratic feature map - not time-integration - is what pays; every arm gets WORSE from T=4 to T=16

result_summary: The pre-registered null was refuted and then the win was re-attributed. (1) SYNC IS NOT DECORATION: at matched core, params (0.46% spread), ticks, steps and batch stream, the CTM synchronization readout beats a last-tick readout on the identical core by +0.056 bit accuracy at T=16 and +0.058 at T=4, fully seed-separated at T=16 (worst sync 0.667 > best last 0.638), and beats an iso-parameter GRU with last-state readout by +0.105, seed-separated at both tick counts. (2) BUT IT IS NOT SYNCHRONIZATION. The added control - the same 256 neuron-pair products evaluated at the LAST TICK ONLY, zero time-integration, same dimensionality, same params - ties sync at T=4 (0.6848 vs 0.6866, a 0.002 gap against a 0.02 seed sd) and trails by only 0.022 at T=16 with fully overlapping seeds (pairlast best 0.675 > sync worst 0.667). Decomposing the sync-over-last gap: the quadratic pair expansion is worth +0.056 (T=4) / +0.034 (T=16), the time-integration on top of it is worth +0.002 (T=4) / +0.022 (T=16, not seed-separated). So roughly 60-100% of the CTM readout's advantage is a fixed random QUADRATIC FEATURE MAP over neuron pairs, not the neuron-timing synchronization the paper names as its central representation. (3) RECURRENCE DEPTH BUYS NOTHING AT THIS BUDGET: every single arm is flat-to-worse from T=4 to T=16 (sync -0.013, last -0.011, gru -0.021, pairlast -0.033, mean -0.063), so the backlog's dichotomy ('sync, or just recurrence depth?') has a third answer here - neither; it is the readout's feature map. (4) TIME-AVERAGING THE HIDDEN STATE IS ACTIVELY HARMFUL: the mean-over-ticks readout loses the most from extra depth and at T=16 drops BELOW the plain last-tick readout, nearly to GRU level - but multiplying neuron pairs and THEN averaging (sync) does not suffer this. (5) The per-neuron history MLPs are load-bearing: last vs gru, same readout and same attention and same params, is +0.049 at T=16. (6) The accuracy differences are entirely 'how deep a prefix does it crack': every arm is at exact chance beyond a cliff and near-perfect below it; effective solved prefix depth at T=16 is sync 4.19, pairlast 3.69, last 2.85, mean 1.87, gru 1.69 out of 12, and final training loss ranks identically (0.444/0.478/0.513/0.569/0.585), so this is optimisation progress, not an eval artifact. CAVEATS, and they are large: heavily shrunk to fit a 12-minute CPU box - 12 bits (backlog asked 24-40), 475 steps, 0.056M params, T<=16 against the paper's 75-100 ticks; NO arm comes close to solving the task (exact match <= 0.007), so every conclusion is about early-training progress at matched compute, not converged performance; one hyperparameter setting (lr 3e-3, batch 64) picked by a short pilot on the sync arm and not tuned per arm; 3 seeds; one fixed 256-pair subset shared by both quadratic arms (pair-subset variance unmeasured). A discarded 2-seed pilot that also covered T=8 reproduces the ordering and the declining depth trend (T=8: sync 0.697, pairlast 0.679, last 0.667, mean 0.618, gru 0.594).

novelty_check.conclusion: The architecture is fully published; this specific ablation is not. The CTM paper (2505.05522, NeurIPS 2025) defines the synchronization matrix S^t = Z^t (Z^t)^T (Eq. 5) and its learnable exponential decay (Eq. 9-10) and runs the 64-length cumulative-parity demo, but its baselines are whole-architecture LSTMs - it never swaps the READOUT on a fixed core. title: Weight tying at nano scale: the benefit-of-tying curve has the wrong sign - tying's cost GROWS with embedding fraction, and untying beats 37% more width
hypothesis: Tying the input embedding to the output unembedding helps only when the vocab/param ratio is high: delta val bpc (tied minus untied) should be negative at high embedding fraction and ~0 or positive at low, with a crossover in between.
question: Is the practitioner rule 'tie small models with big vocabularies, untie big models with small vocabularies' visible as a crossover in the delta-val-bpc-vs-embedding-fraction curve at 0.02-0.3M params, and does it survive a matched-total-parameter control?
method: nanoGPT-style 1-layer pre-norm decoder LM on tiny-shakespeare, trained tied vs untied at 5 grid points spanning embedding fraction 0.07 -> 0.82. The fraction is moved along TWO independent axes: (a) vocab at fixed d_model=64 - char (V=65) vs a hand-rolled greedy BPE fitted on the train split only at V=512 (2.22 chars/token) and V=2000 (3.18 chars/token); (b) d_model in {32,64,128} at fixed char vocab. MATCHING POLICY, stated and applied throughout: PRIMARY = matched architecture (tied and untied share d_model / n_layer / n_head / d_ff / block_size / vocab; the only difference is whether the output projection reuses the token-embedding matrix, so untied carries V*d more params - deliberately, because that is the question a practitioner asks). SECONDARY = matched TOTAL params at both extremes of the axis, where the untied model's d_model is shrunk until its parameter count equals the tied model's (d 128->124, gap -2.2%; d 64->40, gap -0.2%). Iso-everything otherwise: 800 steps, batch 16 x 96 tokens (1.23M tokens), AdamW lr 3e-3 with 80-step warmup and cosine decay to 10%, wd 0.1 on 2-D weights, grad clip 1.0, and an IDENTICAL batch stream for the tied and untied arm at a given (config, seed). 2 seeds per primary point, 1 per control. Metric is val bits per CHARACTER (token NLL in nats / (ln2 * characters those tokens cover)) so numbers are comparable across vocabularies. 22 runs.
architecture: 1-layer pre-norm decoder-only transformer, 4 heads, d_ff = 4*d_model, learned absolute position embeddings, block size 96, no biases, GELU MLP; d_model in {32,40,64,124,128}, vocab in {65,512,2000}, 0.018M-0.312M params

dataset.name: tiny-shakespeare (char stream; BPE vocabs built from the train split itself)
dataset.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt
dataset.license: public domain text; char-rnn repo MIT

task: autoregressive language modelling, val bits/character, tied vs untied input/output embeddings across an embedding-fraction sweep
compute: CPU 1 thread, 615s (10.25 min) for 22 training runs + 26.5s of BPE merge fitting

metrics.headline: delta val bpc (tied - untied) vs embedding fraction 2*V*d/P(untied)
metrics.matching_policy: matched-architecture (primary) + matched-total-params control at the two extremes
metrics.pattern: tying never helps at this scale (delta > 0 at every embedding fraction)
metrics.pairs_where_untied_wins: 10 of 10 (every config, every seed; sign-consistent at all 5 points)

result_summary: REFUTED, with the sign reversed. Across an embedding fraction of 0.07 -> 0.82 built on two independent axes (vocab 65/512/2000 at d=64; d_model 32/64/128 at V=65), tying LOSES at every point and the penalty GROWS with embedding fraction rather than turning into a benefit: delta val bpc (tied - untied) = +0.027 / +0.048 / +0.162 / +0.084 / +0.340 at embedding fraction 0.074 / 0.130 / 0.211 / 0.541 / 0.821, Spearman rho = +0.90, no crossover, and all 10 tied/untied pairs sign-consistent. The 'untied just has more parameters' objection is killed by the matched-total-params control: at embedding fraction 0.82 an untied model forced to shrink from d_model 64 to 40 (183,280 vs 183,680 params, -0.2%) STILL beats the tied d=64 model by 0.308 bpc, while at embedding fraction 0.07 the same control is a wash (+0.007). Decomposed at V=2000: going d=40 -> d=64 buys 0.024 bpc, untying buys 0.340 bpc - those parameters are worth ~14x more in a separate output matrix than in extra residual width. The only surviving piece of the folk rule is that tying is nearly FREE at low embedding fraction, which is the opposite polarity from 'tying helps'. Caveats: heavily undertrained (800 steps / 1.23M tokens, val bpc 2.5-3.5 where a converged tiny char LM reaches ~1.5-1.7) and the tying penalty is an early-training phenomenon in the gradient-imbalance account of 2603.26663, so training length is the caveat most likely to change the sign; 1 layer; 2 seeds (1 for controls); iso-hyperparameter rather than per-arm-tuned LR, which matters because the tied matrix receives the sum of two gradient signals; absolute bpc is not comparable across configs because the BPE arms make ~3 passes over their train split vs ~1.2 for char (the within-config delta is clean - shared batch stream); embedding fraction is confounded with total model size along the d_model axis, so the vocab axis carries most of the evidence.

novelty_check.conclusion: The mechanism is 2016-vintage and fully published; the curve is not. Press & Wolf (1608.05859) and Inan et al. (1611.01462) introduce tying and show it improves perplexity, but at a FIXED vocabulary and architecture - there is no embedding-fraction axis anywhere in either. 'Weight Tying Biases Token Embeddings Towards the Output Space' (2603.26663, 2026) supplies a mechanistic account we can borrow (tied embeddings align with unembeddings; output gradients dominate early training; scaling input gradients reduces the bias) but measures the bias, not the loss delta as a function of embedding fraction. 'Beyond Weight Tying' (W18-6308) relaxes the constraint, again at fixed vocab. The rule this experiment tests - 'tie small models with big vocabularies, untie big ones' / 'at fixed model size the vocabulary determines whether tying is a big deal' - circulates in practitioner writing (blog.silennai.com/tied-embeddings; the Medium explainer), and BOTH were fetched and checked: each presents the parameter-savings arithmetic (20.5% of a 1B model, 2.9% of 7B, 0.3% of 70B) in place of a measured tied-vs-untied loss delta, and neither reports a crossover. To our search no published work sweeps the embedding fraction along two independent axes (vocab size AND d_model) on one corpus and reports delta loss from tying against it, and none pairs that with a matched-total-parameter control at both ends. The specific finding - that the curve has the WRONG SIGN, that tying's cost grows with embedding fraction, and that at ef=0.82 an untied model with 37% less width still wins by 0.31 bpc - is, to our search, unreported. arXiv/OpenAlex APIs 403 from this environment (scripts/novelty_check.py returned 'unchecked'); verdict rests on web search plus three direct page fetches. Scale caveat applies throughout: 0.018-0.312M params, 800 steps, undertrained.

The 'no embedding-fraction ablation in Press & Wolf' claim rests on the paper's known experimental design plus secondary summaries, not a fresh full-text read.

title: Quantized Coconut: a continuous thought survives being squeezed to 2 bits - accuracy vs codebook size is flat from K=inf down to K=4
hypothesis: Putting a VQ-VAE-style vector-quantization bottleneck on each continuous thought of a nano-Coconut model degrades held-out DAG-reachability accuracy as the codebook shrinks, with a knee at some K* above which quantized thoughts match the unquantized continuous baseline (0.873 in the sibling run 2026-07-25_coconut-toy-graph); and the surviving discrete codes carry readable structure (code identity correlates with hop count / reachability).
question: How discrete can a continuous thought be before accuracy drops? Sweep a VQ bottleneck's codebook size K on Coconut's fed-back hidden state and find the K at which quantized thoughts stop matching the continuous baseline - or establish honestly that quantization hurts everywhere / nowhere.
method: Direct follow-up to 2026-07-25_coconut-toy-graph, whose task generator, model skeleton, forward pass and staged curriculum are REUSED VERBATIM (the K=inf arm reproduces the sibling's coconut arm bit-identically, per-seed 0.8350/0.9107, mean 0.8728, which validates the reuse). One 2-layer pre-norm decoder-only transformer (d_model=64, 4 heads, FFN 256, 103,168 params) on synthetic DAG reachability (N=8 nodes, out-degree<=2, E=10 edges, adjacency-slot encoding, 21 prefix tokens; 'is dst reachable from src within 3 hops?', 50/50 balanced, positives stratified over path length 1/2/3), H=3 latent thought slots, Coconut curriculum k=0->1->2 over the first 60% of steps then k=3, AdamW lr 2e-3 (50-step warmup), wd 0.01, grad-clip 1.0, batch 64, 1100 steps, 2 seeds. THE ONE CHANGE: a VQ-VAE bottleneck (arXiv:1711.00937) on every fed-back thought vector - hard argmin nearest-neighbour forward, straight-through estimator backward, codebook loss ||sg[h]-e||^2 + 0.25*||h-sg[e]||^2 at weight 1.0, codebook init N(0,1) per dim and excluded from weight decay, plus dead-code restarts every 100 steps (a code unused since the last restart is reset to a thought vector from the current batch + 0.01 noise) so that large-K arms are not silently small-K arms. VQ was stable in every arm, so the Gumbel-softmax fallback the backlog allowed was not needed. Arms: K in {4,16,64,256} plus unquantized K=inf; 5 arms x 2 seeds = 10 runs. Readability analysis on the 3000 held-out graphs: per-slot codebook usage perplexity 2^H(code), plus normalized mutual information between the emitted code and (a) the YES/NO label, (b) the hop count, (c) the ground-truth BFS path node, each MINUS an identically-computed label-shuffled control that measures the finite-sample MI bias (raw bias up to 0.078 at K=256). Because seed variance (0.038) exceeds every arm effect, the headline statistic is the PAIRED delta - each quantized run minus the continuous run at the same seed - computed from metrics.per_run.
architecture: 2-layer decoder-only transformer, d_model=64, 4 heads, FFN 256, 103,168 params, identical in all five arms; Coconut continuous thought = last hidden state fed back as next input embedding; VQ bottleneck adds K x 64 codebook params (256 at K=4 up to 16,384 at K=256) used only on the 3 fed-back thought vectors

dataset.name: synthetic random DAGs, N=8 nodes, out-degree <= 2, exactly E=10 edges, fixed-width adjacency-slot encoding; yes/no reachability-within-3-hops queries balanced 50/50 and stratified by shortest-path length 1/2/3; 20,000 train / 3,000 held-out graphs from disjoint seeded streams (generator identical to 2026-07-25_coconut-toy-graph)
dataset.source: generated in run.py (numpy PCG64, seeds 1234 / 777001)

task: multi-hop DAG reachability (binary: is dst reachable from src within 3 hops?); negatives are unreachable OR further than 3 hops, so depth must be tracked
compute: CPU single-threaded, 594.3s for all 10 training runs + eval + code-usage analysis

metrics.note_on_pairing: every arm uses the same two seeds, so the same-seed paired mean equals the difference of means; pairing changes the error bar, not the point estimate
metrics.headline: held-out acc vs codebook size: K=inf 0.873, K=256 0.858, K=64 0.826, K=16 0.864, K=4 0.860; the curve is FLAT (paired cost of quantization -0.021 +- 0.024 across 8 comparisons, non-monotone in K), so K* = 4, the smallest codebook swept; a 2-bit thought still beats pause tokens (0.687) and no-CoT (0.600) by +0.17/+0.26; code usage saturates at ~50 effective codes when 256 are offered, and the FIRST thought collapses to 1-3 codes (zero bits in one seed) with no accuracy cost

result_summary: Refuted, and cleanly. The hypothesis predicted a knee: a codebook size below which discretizing Coconut's continuous thought costs accuracy. There is no knee anywhere in the swept range. Held-out accuracy is 0.873 (K=inf, a bit-identical replication of the sibling's coconut arm), 0.858 (K=256), 0.826 (K=64), 0.864 (K=16), 0.860 (K=4). Seed variance (0.038) exceeds every arm effect, so the paired statistic carries the claim: across all 8 same-seed comparisons quantization costs -0.021 accuracy on average (sd 0.024, range +0.007 to -0.072) and the cost is NOT monotone in K - K=64 is the worst arm and K=16 the best quantized one, the signature of noise rather than of an information bottleneck. K* (smallest K matching the continuous baseline within one seed-std) is 4, the smallest codebook swept: two bits per thought, six bits for the entire latent reasoning chain, and a 2-bit thought retains essentially the whole Coconut advantage established by the sibling (0.860 vs 0.687 for compute-matched pause tokens and 0.600 for no-CoT). The codebook statistics say the model never wanted the bandwidth: given 256 codes it uses ~50 effectively (187 ever emitted) and usage perplexity tracks K sublinearly all the way down; the FIRST of the three thoughts is nearly contentless at every K (perplexity 9.3 of 256, 1.5 of 4) and in one K=4 seed collapsed to a single code - literally zero bits - while that run still scored 0.877, i.e. thought 1 is functioning as a pause token and the information lives in thoughts 2 and 3. On the 'readable thoughts' bonus the codes are partially readable but mostly of the ANSWER, not the search state: shuffle-corrected normalized MI is 0.45-0.55 with the YES/NO label, 0.26-0.33 with the hop count, and only 0.17-0.24 with the BFS path node (itself inflated by NONE-padding leakage), consistently across K. Taken with the sibling's finding that the thought is not a linearly-readable BFS frontier, the picture is that Coconut's latent step at this scale is a low-bandwidth commitment signal ('which branch, found it yet') rather than a rich continuous superposition of reasoning paths - good news for interpretability, since a 2-bit thought is enumerable. Practical corollary: the large codebooks used in the literature (64-1024 in Token Assorted, 2.5k-40k in DLR) may be far more than latent reasoning needs; start small and check whether the model asks for more. Caveats: the VQ bottlenecks the thought CHANNEL only - the final thought position still attends to the whole prefix through the KV cache, so the model can re-read the graph, which is why 'K=4 is fine' is less surprising than it sounds; 2 seeds; 103k params, 1100 steps, one task; dead-code restarts (1387 fired at K=256) are load-bearing for the large-K arms and deviate from vanilla VQ-VAE; MI is a plug-in estimate with a first-order shuffle correction.

novelty_check.conclusion: VQ-on-latent-reasoning exists; the small-K end of the curve does not. Token Assorted / 'Mixing Latent and Text Tokens' (2502.03275) applies a VQ-VAE to reasoning traces but fixes the codebook per benchmark (64 ProntoQA/ProsQA, 512 maze, 1024 math) - the fetch confirmed it ablates the compression rate r instead of K, and never compares against unquantized COCONUT directly (only a 'Curriculum-Replace' proxy). DLR / 'Why Struggle with Continuous Latents?' (2606.29712) DOES sweep the codebook, K in {2.5k,5k,10k,20k,40k}, finding improvement to 10k then plateau - but it quantizes rendered-image OCR features of a textual CoT at LLM scale, and its smallest codebook is 2500, three orders of magnitude above the regime where we find the curve is already flat. To our search nobody has quantized Coconut's own fed-back hidden state directly and swept K down to 4 against a matched unquantized control on the same task, model, seeds and curriculum. The specific findings - flat accuracy from K=inf to K=4 (paired cost -0.021 +- 0.024), a 2-bit thought retaining the full +0.26 advantage over no-CoT, codebook usage saturating at ~50 effective codes when 256 are offered, and the first thought collapsing to 1-3 codes (zero bits in one seed) at no cost - are unreported to our search. arXiv/OpenAlex APIs 403 from this environment, so the verdict rests on WebSearch plus two direct paper fetches. title: Head dim vs head count at fixed d_model: no U-curve - val bpc is perfectly monotone in head_dim, one giant head ties the best, and tiny heads go DIFFUSE not sharp
hypothesis: At fixed d_model=128 a moderate head_dim beats both extremes (1 giant head, many tiny heads), producing a clean iso-parameter U-curve in validation bits-per-character.
question: Sweeping (n_head, head_dim) over the exactly-iso-parameter family n_head * head_dim = d_model = 128, is the val-bpc-vs-head_dim curve a U (interior optimum), a monotone trend, or flat within seed noise - and do tiny heads collapse to sharp single-token attention?
method: nanoGPT-style 2-layer pre-norm decoder-only char LM on tiny-shakespeare at d_model=128, trained at six head splits (n_head, head_dim) = (1,128), (2,64), (4,32), (8,16), (16,8), (32,4). MATCHING POLICY: this family is iso-parameter BY CONSTRUCTION and needs no matching heuristic - at fixed d_model the attention block is d->3d for qkv and d->d for the output projection regardless of the split, so all six arms have identical parameter counts (verified: one count, 423,424, across all 12 runs). It is iso-FLOP for the same reason: the T x T score matrix is computed n_head times over head_dim channels and n_head * head_dim = d. Because all arms share module SHAPES, seeding the constructor identically makes the six arms bit-identical at init (verified via a summed-|weight| signature), and each seed replays an identical batch stream, so the comparison is tightly paired: the only difference between two arms is how the same q/k/v vectors are reshaped before the softmax, plus the 1/sqrt(head_dim) score scale that follows. Iso-hyperparameter otherwise: 600 steps, batch 16 x 96 tokens (0.92M tokens/run), AdamW lr 3e-3 with 60-step warmup and cosine decay to 10%, wd 0.1 on 2-D weights, grad clip 1.0, d_ff = 4*d_model, learned absolute positions, no biases. 2 seeds x 6 configs = 12 runs. Metric is val bits per character on a fixed 46,080-char held-out slice. Mechanistic side-probe after training: per-head causal attention entropy on fixed val batches, normalised by the uniform-over-prefix entropy (H_t / ln(t+1), positions t >= 8), plus mean top-1 attention weight and effective keys attended (exp H).

metrics.headline: val bpc vs head_dim at fixed d_model=128 (exactly iso-parameter)
metrics.matching_policy: iso-parameter by construction (n_head * head_dim = d_model); additionally identical init and identical batch stream across arms per seed

result_summary: REFUTED - there is no U-curve and no interior optimum. Across the exactly-iso-parameter family n_head * head_dim = 128 (all six arms 423,424 params, bit-identical at init, identical batch stream), mean val bpc is PERFECTLY monotone in head_dim: 2.8759 / 2.8868 / 2.9254 / 3.0237 / 3.0623 / 3.0929 at head_dim 128 / 64 / 32 / 16 / 8 / 4, Spearman(log2 head_dim, bpc) = -1.00. The config spread of 0.217 bpc is 9.65x the mean within-config seed spread (0.0225), so the effect is ~10 seed-widths. The 'many tiny heads are bad' half of the hypothesis holds; the 'one giant head is bad' half does not - the head_dim=128 end IS the optimum (edge gap 0.0). The honest refinement is that the top of the curve is a PLATEAU, not a peak: head_dim 128 vs 64 differ by only 0.011 bpc, inside the 0.064 seed range of the 64 arm, and the two seeds disagree on which wins (seed 0 ranks 64 first, seed 1 ranks 128 first). So head_dim >= 64 is free and head_dim <= 32 is a monotone tax (+0.050 / +0.148 / +0.187 / +0.217 bpc). Train loss orders identically to val loss (1.912 -> 2.098 nats), so this is a fitting/optimisation deficit at matched steps, not a generalisation gap. MECHANISTIC PROBE COMES OUT BACKWARDS: tiny heads do not collapse to sharp single-token attention, they get BLURRIER - normalised attention entropy H/ln(t+1) climbs 0.624 (head_dim=64) -> 0.742 (head_dim=4), mean top-1 attention weight falls 0.335 -> 0.232, effective keys attended rises 15.6 -> 25.5, Spearman(log2 head_dim, entropy) = -0.83; a 4-dimensional QK space appears unable to express sharply peaked content-selective scores, so most tiny heads drift toward near-uniform averaging. The tiny-head population is heterogeneous, though: at head_dim=4 per-head normalised entropy spans 0.235-0.994 and the single sharpest head beats anything in the 1-head model (max top-1 weight 0.749 vs 0.487) - a few sharp heads plus a majority of near-uniform ones. Caveats: (1) heavily undertrained - 600 steps / 0.92M tokens leaves every arm at bpc 2.88-3.09 where a converged tiny char LM reaches ~1.5-1.7, so part of the many-heads deficit may be slower learning rather than a lower ceiling; (2) the softmax temperature 1/sqrt(head_dim) varies by 5.7x across the sweep - inherent to the standard formulation, but it means 'low-rank bottleneck' and 'wrong score temperature' are not separated here, and a QK-norm control is the direct next experiment; (3) 2 layers, 2 seeds, one corpus, one lr (3e-3) shared by all arms rather than per-arm tuned; (4) block size 96 sits between the head_dim=64 and head_dim=128 arms, so the Bhojanapalli 'head_dim >= sequence length' threshold cannot be resolved sharply - the observed knee is at head_dim ~32-64, not exactly at 96.

novelty_check.conclusion: The axis is published; this scale, this resolution, and the entropy fingerprint are not. Bhojanapalli et al. (2002.07028, ICML 2020) is the direct prior art and was fetched in full: it sweeps heads 8 -> 16 -> 32 at fixed embedding size 1024 in BERT_LARGE and reports degradation past 8 heads (SQuAD F1 90.89 -> 90.45), with the theoretical claim that the bottleneck bites once head_dim < sequence length and a fix (head size decoupled from head count) under which more heads then help monotonically. That is the same monotone direction we find, at 340M params, 3 grid points, and head_dim 32-128. 'Leaner Transformers: More Heads, Less Depth' (2505.20802) was also fetched and is NOT this axis - it holds head_dim fixed and lets d_model grow with head count at varying parameter budgets, and reports no interior optimum. Michel et al. ('Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?') prunes heads after training rather than ablating the split. Zhai et al. (2303.06296) uses attention entropy as a training-stability diagnostic, as a function of dynamics and sigma-Reparam, not of head_dim. To our search, nobody has run this family at nano scale with 6 grid points spanning the fully degenerate range (1 head through head_dim=4), with an exactly iso-parameter identical-init shared-batch-stream paired design, and the two specific findings appear unreported: (a) the curve is monotone with a PLATEAU at head_dim >= 64 rather than the interior optimum the folk U-curve asserts, and (b) the attention-entropy signature runs opposite to intuition - tiny heads attend more DIFFUSELY (entropy 0.62 -> 0.74, top-1 weight 0.34 -> 0.23), a mechanistic fingerprint of the low-rank bottleneck that the original paper does not measure. arXiv/OpenAlex APIs 403 from this environment (scripts/novelty_check.py returned 'unchecked'); verdict rests on 4 web searches plus 2 direct paper fetches. Scale caveat throughout: 0.42M params, 600 steps, undertrained.

title: Trained PonderNet halting vs stochastic depth for LENGTH generalization: the halt head learns real difficulty (allocation extrapolates 5x, +0.130 over stochastic depth at MATCHED compute, +0.145 over a compute-matched random exit) but stochastic depth is simply PERFECT at 5x train length (1.000 token acc AND 1.000 exact match), so the ceiling is not adaptive
hypothesis: On an n-RASP-L-style task whose required number of sequential steps grows linearly with input length (prefix-parity under a 2-token attention window: position i needs K >= i-1 loops), a weight-tied block trained with a PonderNet halting head learns to spend MORE loops on longer inputs and therefore extrapolates further in LENGTH than the same block trained at a fixed loop count - and at least matches the proven stochastic-depth recipe (k ~ U{1..K_train}).
question: Does TRAINED halting (learned per-step halt probability with PonderNet expected-loss weighting and a KL to a geometric prior) succeed where the INFERENCE-TIME entropy halting of 2026-07-25_shadow-halt-entropy-tiny failed - and does it match or beat the stochastic-depth recipe of 2026-07-25_loop-test-time-compute on LENGTH (not just depth) generalization?
method: Task engineered so that required depth is an ANALYTIC GROUND TRUTH PER POSITION. Prefix-parity (cumulative XOR): input [BOS, x_1..x_L], target y_i = XOR(x_1..x_i), with BANDED CAUSAL attention of WINDOW 1 - every position attends only to itself and its immediate predecessor - so after K applications of the tied block position i has only seen bits [i-K, i] and position i is solvable IFF K >= i-1. A length-L input therefore requires exactly L-1 loops, length generalization and depth generalization are the same axis by construction, and the halting head's allocation can be scored against truth as a SLOPE (measured 0.68 vs required 1.0) rather than judged only by downstream accuracy. Architecture: one pre-LN transformer block, d_model 64, 2 heads, d_ff 256, NoPE, weight-tied and applied K times with recurrent-depth-style per-iteration input injection (adapter on [h ; e]); 58,370 params, the two ponder arms adding a 65-param halt head (+0.11%). NoPE rather than ALiBi (which 2026-07-25_pe-length-gen-tiny ranked best) because inside a 2-token band a distance bias is a no-op and XOR over the window is order-invariant, so NoPE here means no position information at all - the strongest available length-extrapolation prior for this task. Four arms x 2 seeds = 8 runs, all with identical hyperparameters (1000 steps, batch 128, AdamW lr 2e-3 with 100-step warmup + cosine, wd 0.01, grad clip 1.0): (a) fixed_K7 - fixed K=7, lengths L ~ U{2..8}; (b) stoch_depth - the proven recipe, k ~ U{1..7} per batch with L = k+1 so every supervised position is exactly computable at that depth; (c) ponder - PonderNet with a per-position halt head over N=7 unrolled steps, loss sum_n p_n * CE_n + 0.01 * KL(p || truncated Geom(0.2)), lengths L ~ U{2..8}; (d) ponder_stoch - crossed hybrid, PonderNet loss with a STOCHASTIC unroll horizon N ~ U{L-1..7}, which is the only way to answer 'is stochastic depth all you need' rather than 'is PonderNet worse'. Evaluation: train lengths <= 8, test lengths up to 40 (5x extrapolation; the deepest position needs 39 loops), K_max_test = 40, 384 fixed held-out sequences from a disjoint seed. Because attention is causal the prediction at position i is identical for any total length >= i, so ONE length-40 batch yields every shorter length EXACTLY; this is asserted in code by prefix_consistency_check against a genuine short batch and passes for all 8 runs. Four inference policies reported: cumulative halting probability >= 0.5 (primary; the median of the learned halting distribution), lambda_n >= 0.5, argmax p_n, and seeded Bernoulli sampling - they agree within 0.013. TWO CONTROLS carry the argument: (i) a threshold sweep tracing an accuracy-vs-compute frontier for the learned signal against a COMPUTE-MATCHED RANDOM EXIT (per-step geometric halting, zero information about difficulty), interpolated to identical mean loops - the exact control that killed inference-time entropy halting in 2026-07-25_shadow-halt-entropy-tiny; and (ii) an ISO-COMPUTE comparison interpolating every arm's fixed-K frontier to the adaptive arm's mean loops per position, because the naive table gives the fixed arms 40 loops and the adaptive arm only the ~18 it chooses.
architecture: one weight-tied pre-LN transformer block, d_model 64, 2 heads, d_ff 256, banded causal attention window 1, NoPE, per-iteration input injection adapter on [h ; e], final LayerNorm + 2-way readout; 58,370 params (58,435 with the PonderNet halt head)

task: n-RASP-L-style prefix-parity; token accuracy and whole-sequence exact match vs TEST LENGTH per arm (train L<=8, test L<=40), mean loops used per length for the adaptive arms, and halt step vs position against the analytic requirement i-1

metrics.headline: token accuracy and exact match vs test LENGTH at 5x train length (train L<=8, test L=40, 39 loops required), adaptive halting vs stochastic depth
metrics.verdict: hypothesis refuted on the ceiling, confirmed on the mechanism

result_summary: TWO-SIDED, and which side matters depends on whether you can afford max depth. (1) STOCHASTIC DEPTH IS SIMPLY PERFECT AND WINS THE CEILING. Trained with k ~ U{1..7} and L=k+1 on lengths <=8, the 58,370-param tied block scores 1.000 token accuracy AND 1.000 whole-sequence exact match at EVERY test length from 2 to 40 - 5x the longest training length, 39 loops required at the deepest position - on both seeds and at all 40 positions. The best adaptive arm reaches 0.866 / 0.505, i.e. -0.134 token accuracy and -0.495 exact match. So the backlog's 'stochastic depth is all you need' outcome is what happened. (2) BUT TRAINED HALTING IS EMPHATICALLY NOT THE NULL THAT INFERENCE-TIME HALTING WAS - this is the direct answer to 2026-07-25_shadow-halt-entropy-tiny. The PonderNet halt head, trained only on positions 1-8, learns a difficulty-tracking allocation that EXTRAPOLATES 5x: mean halt step climbs monotonically 3.0 (position 1) -> 29.1 (position 40), E[steps] 3.1 -> 29.2. It does not collapse to a fixed depth and it does not collapse to max depth (only 2.2% of positions run all 40 loops - the shallow-collapse and max-collapse failure modes were both predicted and both absent). Against the SAME compute-matched RANDOM-EXIT control that killed entropy halting, the learned signal wins by +0.105 to +0.157 token accuracy at EVERY point on its threshold-swept frontier (mean +0.145), where entropy halting had been <= 0. The difference between a worthless halting signal and a useful one is training it. (3) AT MATCHED COMPUTE THE ORDERING INVERTS AND ADAPTIVE WINS OUTRIGHT. The headline table gives the fixed arms 40 loops and the adaptive arm the 17.9 it chooses. Interpolating every arm's fixed-K frontier to 17.9 loops at L=40: ponder-ADAPTIVE 0.8662 vs stoch_depth fixed-K 0.7365 (+0.130), fixed_K7 0.7318 (+0.134), ponder's own fixed-K frontier 0.7222 (+0.144), random exit 0.7136 (+0.153). Same at L=20 (+0.156). Adaptive halting is a genuine accuracy-per-loop Pareto win over every non-adaptive arm; it buys 55% fewer loops for -0.071 accuracy against running the same weights to K=40. (4) WHY THE CEILING IS STILL LOST: THE SLOPE IS 0.68 AND NEEDS TO BE 1.0. Required loops per position is exactly i-1 (slope 1.0, intercept -1); the learned allocation is slope 0.68, intercept ~+2.4, so the head OVER-spends in distribution and UNDER-spends out of it, crossing the requirement at i~11 and buying 29 loops at position 40 where 39 are needed. Any policy that halts early is capped below 1.000 by construction on this task. (5) MECHANISM: PONDERNET'S EXPECTED LOSS STARVES THE DEEP STEPS. The learned hazard lambda_n rises 0.007 -> 0.409 over 40 steps, so the halting distribution concentrates mass early - and that same p_n is what weights the gradient in sum_n p_n * CE_n, leaving deep-step readouts undertrained, whereas stochastic depth weights every depth 1..K equally. The crossed hybrid confirms it by making things WORSE, not better: ponder_stoch is the worst arm at every long length (0.876 / 0.389 at L=40) and is the only arm to break IN-DISTRIBUTION depth-invariance, its L=8 accuracy decaying 1.000 -> 0.902 as test loops go 14 -> 40. The halting objective also costs the underlying model outright: ponder at K=40 is 0.937 against stoch_depth's 1.000. (6) INCIDENTAL CORRECTION TO OUR OWN REGISTRY: 'fixed-K training fails past its trained depth' (2026-07-25_loop-test-time-compute, frontier 1.00 -> 0.55) is really 'fixed-K with training LENGTH locked to training DEPTH fails'. Here fixed_K7 trained on L ~ U{2..8} reaches 0.925 at L=40, because easy positions must stay correct through 7 loops, which is already an implicit depth-invariance pressure. It remains the weakest non-adaptive arm on exact match (0.616 vs 1.000) and the least seed-stable (1.000 / 0.850), and its per-position accuracy carries a curious even/odd oscillation at large positions (~0.82 odd vs ~0.90 even) that the stochastic arm does not have. CAVEATS: 2 seeds, one task, one architecture; ponder's adaptive accuracy at L=40 is bimodal across seeds (0.732, 1.000) and one ponder seed does match stoch_depth, whereas the stoch_depth result (1.000/1.000 both seeds, all positions) is the tight one; stoch_depth's training length marginal comes from L=k+1 rather than an independent draw (the literal published recipe, and it is the winning arm, so the confound cannot manufacture its length-axis gap, but the data distribution is not fully matched); 'mean loops used' is an analytic compute proxy measured from halting decisions while all positions are computed to K_max, no wall-clock saving is claimed; and the geometric prior (lambda_p=0.2, beta=0.01) is the PonderNet default and was NOT tuned - a prior matched to the task's true mean depth is the most likely way to raise the 0.68 slope and is untested.

novelty_check.conclusion: The mechanism, the task family and the head-to-head each exist in the literature; the combination and the controls do not. 2409.15647 (Looped Transformers for Length Generalization, UW-Madison-Lee-Lab/looped-tf) is the n-RASP-L source and was fetched in full: it trains looped transformers on parity/copy/binary-addition at lengths 1-20 and tests past 40 with GPT-2 blocks at d=256 and NoPE, but its stopping rules are an ORACLE ('assume the number of steps needed is given') or a MAXIMUM-CONFIDENCE criterion - it does NOT train a halting head and does NOT compare against a stochastic-depth schedule. 2107.05407 (PonderNet) supplies the halting mechanism itself and claims extrapolation success. 2606.29983 ('Stabilizing Extrapolation in Looped Transformers via Learned Stochastic Stopping') is the closest head-to-head and was fetched: its RL-Halting learns a stopping distribution by REINFORCE and does evaluate length generalization (train n<20, test n>=20) on binary addition / Dyck-1 / unique-set / copy with 3-layer tied transformers against hand-designed stochastic schedules - but the halting is REINFORCE-trained rather than PonderNet, and there is no compute-matched random-exit control. 2607.20519 ('Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts') is a title-level match and probably the nearest work, but could NOT be verified - arxiv.org/abs and /html both returned proxy 429/403 across five attempts, the same unavailability flagged in 2026-07-25_shadow-halt-entropy-tiny - so it stands as an unresolved prior-art risk. What appears unreported: (i) required depth known ANALYTICALLY PER POSITION via a window-1 attention band, which lets the halting head's allocation be scored as a slope (0.68 measured against 1.0 required) instead of inferred from downstream accuracy; (ii) the compute-matched RANDOM-EXIT control - the control that killed inference-time entropy halting in our own registry - applied to a TRAINED halting head, which it passes (+0.145 mean) while the arm still loses the ceiling; (iii) a direct PonderNet-vs-stochastic-depth head-to-head at 0.058M params on CPU with the crossed hybrid arm; (iv) the iso-compute inversion (adaptive +0.130 over stochastic depth's fixed-K frontier at matched mean loops, while -0.134 at max compute); (v) the mechanistic diagnosis that the expected-loss weighting starves deep-step readouts, evidenced by the hybrid breaking in-distribution depth-invariance; (vi) the correction that fixed-K training does NOT fail when the training length distribution is decoupled from the training depth. arXiv/OpenAlex APIs 403 from this environment (scripts/novelty_check.py returned 'unchecked'); the verdict rests on 5 web searches plus 3 successful full-text fetches. The 'no prior compute-matched random-exit control on a trained halting head' claim is a negative search result, not an exhaustive review, and is weakened by the unverifiable 2607.20519.

title: SwiGLU vs GELU at equal parameters: the edge does NOT shrink - 78% of the folk margin survives the iso-param correction, and the extra 31% of params buys almost nothing
hypothesis: SwiGLU's edge over GELU shrinks (or vanishes into seed noise) once d_ff is cut by the standard 2/3 factor so that the three-matrix GLU FFN has the same parameter count as the two-matrix baseline; the commonly demoed SwiGLU-at-4x win is substantially a parameter-count artefact.
question: At matched parameters (GELU with d_ff = 4*d_model vs SwiGLU with d_ff = (8/3)*d_model), is the SwiGLU advantage in val bits-per-character seed-separated or noise - and what fraction of the margin shown by the UNFAIR demo comparison (SwiGLU at d_ff = 4*d_model, +31% params) is bought with parameters rather than with the gating nonlinearity?
method: nanoGPT-style 2-layer pre-norm decoder-only char LM on tiny-shakespeare at d_model=128, 4 heads, block size 96, learned absolute positions, no biases, untied head. Only the FFN block varies, over four arms: (a) gelu_4x = W2.gelu(Wx) at d_ff=512; (b) swiglu_iso = W2.(silu(Wx) * Vx) at d_ff=341, i.e. Shazeer's standard 2/3 correction d_ff=(8/3)*d_model=341.33 rounded down; (c) swiglu_4x = same GLU FFN at d_ff=512, the parameter-advantaged comparison most tutorials and blog demos actually run; (d) relu_4x = W2.relu(Wx) at d_ff=512, the old-school reference. MATCHING POLICY: a GLU FFN has three weight matrices (gate W, up V, down W2) where a vanilla FFN has two, so at equal d_ff it carries 1.5x the FFN weights; setting d_ff=(8/3)*d for the GLU arm equalises both parameters (3*d*(8d/3) = 8d^2 = 2*d*4d) and forward MACs. Verified in-run and asserted, not assumed: the iso pair is 423,424 (gelu_4x) vs 423,168 (swiglu_iso), a relative difference of 0.0605%, well inside the 1% tolerance; FFN MACs/token are 262,144 vs 261,888. The rounding of 341.33 down to 341 leaves swiglu_iso 256 parameters BELOW the baseline, i.e. very slightly handicapped rather than favoured. swiglu_4x carries +30.96% total parameters and +50% FFN parameters. Init cannot be shared across arms (the FFN shapes differ by construction), so pairing is achieved instead by replaying an IDENTICAL batch stream across all four arms at each seed, and the per-seed spread is used as the error bar. Iso-hyperparameter otherwise: 700 steps, batch 16 x 96 tokens (1.075M tokens/run), AdamW lr 3e-3 with 70-step warmup and cosine decay to 10%, wd 0.1 on 2-D weights, grad clip 1.0. 3 seeds x 4 arms = 12 runs. Metric is val bits per character on a fixed 46,080-char held-out slice. Post-hoc derived analysis from the stored training curves and per-run seconds: an approximate wall-clock-matched comparison (who is ahead inside gelu_4x's training-time budget), reported as indicative because it uses train loss and truncates a cosine schedule written for 700 steps.
architecture: 2-layer pre-norm decoder-only transformer, d_model=128, 4 heads, block size 96, learned absolute positions, no biases, untied output head; FFN swapped between 2-matrix (gelu/relu) and 3-matrix GLU (silu gate); 423,424 params for gelu_4x and relu_4x, 423,168 for swiglu_iso, 554,496 for swiglu_4x

metrics.headline: val bpc, GELU-4x vs SwiGLU-8/3x at matched parameters, with the param-advantaged SwiGLU-4x and ReLU-4x alongside

wall_clock_matched_approx.note: indicative only: uses smoothed TRAIN bpc and truncates a cosine schedule written for 700 steps

result_summary: HYPOTHESIS REFUTED - the iso-parameter control does not dissolve SwiGLU's advantage, it removes about a fifth of it. At exactly matched parameters (423,424 for GELU-4x vs 423,168 for SwiGLU-8/3x, 0.0605% apart, and iso-MAC to 0.1%) SwiGLU wins by -0.1379 val bpc (2.7113 vs 2.8492), with all three seeds agreeing in sign and the gap at 2.99x the mean within-arm seed spread (0.0462) - verdict 'seed-separated'. THE NUMBER THIS EXPERIMENT EXISTS TO PRODUCE: the unfair demo comparison (SwiGLU at d_ff=4*d_model, +30.96% total params, +50% FFN params) beats GELU-4x by -0.1770 bpc, so 77.9% of the folk margin SURVIVES the parameter correction and only 22.1% is attributable to parameter count. The premise behind the hypothesis is wrong here by roughly 4x. Equivalently: growing SwiGLU from d_ff=341 to d_ff=512 (+31% params, +50% FFN FLOPs) buys just 0.039 bpc, less than the mean seed spread - the extra width is nearly worthless while the gating is worth 0.138. The arm ranking is IDENTICAL in every seed: swiglu_4x 2.6722 < swiglu_iso 2.7113 < relu_4x 2.7966 < gelu_4x 2.8492, no seed inverts any pair. SECONDARY FINDING: ReLU-4x beats GELU-4x at identical parameters by 0.0526 bpc in all three seeds - Shazeer's Table 1 has ReLU nominally ahead of GELU too (1.677 vs 1.679) but inside noise; here the sign is consistent and the gap is about one seed spread, so at this scale GELU is the weakest of the three activations tested and the ReLU->GELU step of the folk progression is much less load-bearing than the vanilla->gated step. MECHANISM: this is a fitting effect, not a regularisation effect - train loss orders exactly like val loss (1.888 gelu / 1.838 relu / 1.757 swiglu_iso / 1.735 swiglu_4x nats), so the gated FFN fits faster at the same parameter count rather than generalising better. WALL CLOCK: iso-param and iso-MAC is not iso-seconds - three skinnier GEMMs plus an elementwise product cost 1.135x GELU's seconds/step, and swiglu_4x costs 1.559x. Inside GELU's 48.8s budget swiglu_iso completes 616/700 steps and is still ahead by -0.127 train bpc (the win survives a CPU-seconds budget), but swiglu_4x completes only 448 steps and is +0.090 WORSE than GELU at matched seconds - the param-advantaged configuration wins per step and loses per second. Caveats: (1) EARLY TRAINING - 700 steps / 1.08M tokens leaves every arm at bpc 2.67-2.85 against a converged tiny char LM's ~1.5-1.7, so what is measured is fitting speed at matched parameters and a faster-fitting arm need not have a lower ceiling; (2) one learning rate (3e-3) shared by all arms rather than per-arm tuned, and gated FFNs change the effective gradient scale, so part of the margin could be that 3e-3 suits SwiGLU better - a per-arm LR sweep is the cleanest next control; (3) 2 layers, one width, one corpus, 3 seeds; (4) the wall-clock-matched panel uses train loss and truncates a cosine schedule written for 700 steps, so it under-serves the truncated arms and is indicative only.

novelty_check.conclusion: REPLICATION, and the backlog's framing needs correcting: the iso-parameter control is not something the source paper skips - Shazeer (2002.05202) applies it explicitly and states it verbatim ('To keep the number of parameters and the amount of computation constant, we reduce the number of hidden units d_ff ... by a factor of 2/3'). The PDF was fetched: Table 1 heldout log-perplexity at 524,288 steps is FFN_ReLU 1.677, FFN_GELU 1.679, FFN_SwiGLU 1.636, with ~+-0.005 inter-run std reported over 4 runs at 65,536 steps, i.e. an iso-param SwiGLU margin of ~0.043 log-ppl at ~8x run-to-run std. Our -0.138 bpc at 2.99x seed spread is the same qualitative result at four orders of magnitude smaller scale, so this run is a faithful tiny-CPU replication rather than a discovery. Narang et al. (2102.11972, EMNLP 2021) was also fetched and is the strongest independent corroboration: an audit that found MOST transformer modifications do not transfer, with GLU variants among the small set that did ('SwiGLU and GeGLU improve performance on pre-training, fine-tuning, and supervised training without sacrificing any efficiency in terms of speed'), under a design where 'each variant has approximately the same number of parameters or total operations as the vanilla Transformer'. What the search did NOT surface, and what this row therefore contributes: (a) the corrected and uncorrected comparisons run SIDE BY SIDE so the demoed margin can be decomposed into gating (77.9%) vs parameter count (22.1%) - the single number a practitioner reading an uncorrected blog demo would want, and one we could not find published anywhere; (b) the whole control at nano scale (0.42M params, CPU, 12 min) with all three seeds reported individually; (c) a consistent-sign ReLU > GELU ordering at iso-param, which the source paper leaves inside its noise band. arXiv and OpenAlex APIs both 403 from this environment (scripts/novelty_check.py returned 'unchecked'); verdict rests on 5 web searches plus 2 direct paper fetches. title: Loops do NOT track parse depth: on length-matched ListOps-mini no arm's optimal loop count grows with nesting depth, and the stochastic-depth recipe that wins on serial tasks is the WORST arm here
hypothesis: The stochastic-depth recipe that turned a weight-tied loop into a real test-time-compute axis on a SERIAL task (registry 2026-07-25_loop-test-time-compute, 2026-07-26_looped-halt-nrasp) extends to a HIERARCHICAL one: a tied block trained on ListOps nesting depth 1-4 with k~U{1..4} keeps improving on unseen depth 5-6 expressions when given more loops at test time, and loop iteration t resolves nesting level t.
question: On nested-expression evaluation, does a weight-tied looped transformer buy accuracy on expressions DEEPER than it was trained on by running more loops at test time - and is its optimal test-time loop count a function of the input's parse depth? Does stochastic-depth training transfer from serial structure to tree structure, and does loop iteration t resolve nesting level t?
method: ListOps-mini: nested prefix expressions over digits 0-9 with ops MAX/MIN/MED (SUM_MOD dropped per the backlog item; MED = floor median so answers stay in 0-9), generated synthetically and seeded in listops.py. 10-way classification of the root value read off a prepended [CLS] token. 40,000 deduplicated training expressions at nesting depth 1-4; 384 held-out expressions per depth for depths 1-6, asserted disjoint from train. THE CONTROL THIS EXPERIMENT EXISTS FOR: depth and length are DECOUPLED. A depth-6 tree is naturally longer than a depth-2 tree, so the naive setup confounds depth extrapolation with plain LENGTH extrapolation - and this registry already recorded (2026-07-26_looped-halt-nrasp) that fixed-K fails only when train length is locked to train depth. Here every expression at every depth is grown, by appending extra digit arguments and shallow sibling subtrees that provably cannot raise the tree's height, to a target token length drawn from the SAME band [25,34]; measured mean expression length is 29.68/29.53/29.61/29.62/29.63/29.44 tokens at depth 1/2/3/4/5/6, matched to 0.8%, so depth-5-6 test expressions are length-in-distribution. Architecture: ONE pre-LN transformer block, d_model 96, 4 heads, d_ff 384, BIDIRECTIONAL attention with PAD masking, learned absolute positions, applied K times weight-tied with recurrent-depth-style per-iteration input injection (adapter on [h ; e]), final LayerNorm + 10-way head at position 0; 136,138 parameters, IDENTICAL in every arm. Because the readout is ln_f+head applied to the iterate, reading the answer out at iteration t of one K=8 forward pass is bit-identical to having run at K=t, so the whole accuracy(depth,K) table costs one pass. Three arms at matched params, matched 700 steps, matched batch stream per seed, 2 seeds: (a) fixed_k4 - always 4 loops, loss on the last; (b) stoch_k1to4 - k~U{1..4} per batch, loss on the last; (c) deepsup_k4 - always 4 loops, loss at EVERY iteration (the 2026-07-25_filler-vs-recur probe). The backlog's arm (c), 'K scaled to parse depth at TEST time only', needs no extra training and is read off the table at K=d and K=d+2. Baselines: chance 0.10, per-depth majority class, and the one that matters - the structure-blind BAG-OF-DIGITS SHORTCUT (apply the ROOT operator to the flat multiset of every digit in the expression), which scores 1.000/0.550/0.443/0.378/0.344/0.354 at depths 1-6. AdamW lr 3e-3 (90-step warmup + cosine to 10%), wd 0.01, grad clip 1.0, batch 64. Bonus probe: multinomial logistic probe on the latent at every subtree's ']' token for that subtree's value, per loop iteration t x subtree height h, on the stoch_k1to4 seed-0 model, 70/30 split, <=1200 subtrees per height.
architecture: weight-tied looped transformer block, d_model 96, 4 heads, d_ff 384, bidirectional attention, learned absolute positions, recurrent-depth input injection adapter, CLS readout; 136,138 params identical across all three arms

metrics.headline: accuracy at nesting depth 5-6 (beyond training) per arm, and whether test-time loops K>K_train buy anything on deeper expressions

length_control.note: depth and length decoupled by construction; depth 5-6 is length-in-distribution

probe.note: subtree values ARE weakly decodable (0.40 at h=1 vs majority 0.22; 0.50 at h=6 vs 0.17) but decodability is flat in iteration and the argmax iteration by height is 5,5,3,2,2,5 - nothing on the t=h diagonal

result_summary: HYPOTHESIS REFUTED ON ALL THREE COUNTS, and the negative is clean because depth was decoupled from LENGTH by construction (mean expression length 29.4-29.7 tokens at every depth 1-6, matched to 0.8%) - so a depth-5-6 test expression is length-in-distribution and this is a test of parse-depth extrapolation alone. (1) EXTRA TEST-TIME LOOPS DO NOT HELP ON DEEPER EXPRESSIONS. At depths 5-6, gain from the best K>4 over K=K_train is -0.1641 (fixed_k4), -0.0052 (stoch_k1to4) and +0.0097 (deepsup_k4) - the only positive is inside its own 0.025-0.035 seed spread. fixed_k4 peaks exactly at its trained K=4 (0.5898 at depths 5-6) and collapses on either side (0.30-0.35 at K=5,6; 0.20 at K=8; -0.3252 in-distribution at K=8). (2) NO ARM'S OPTIMAL K GROWS WITH PARSE DEPTH - the central claim of the backlog item. best-K by depth 1..6 is 4,4,4,4,4,4 (fixed_k4), 3,2,2,2,2,2 (stoch_k1to4), 4,3,4,2,3,2 (deepsup_k4): the optimum is pinned to the training schedule or to 2, never to the input's depth. Scored directly at depths 5-6, the 'scale K with parse depth' policy K=d gives 0.3281 vs 0.5898 for flat K=4 on fixed_k4 (-0.2617, i.e. matching loops to depth costs a quarter of the accuracy), 0.4134 vs 0.4200 on stoch (-0.0066) and 0.5645 vs 0.5548 on deepsup (+0.0097). K=d+2 is worse than K=d in every arm. (3) THE STOCHASTIC-DEPTH RECIPE DOES NOT TRANSFER FROM SERIAL TO HIERARCHICAL STRUCTURE - the sharpest result. On prefix-parity the same recipe on the same size of tied block took frontier accuracy 0.55 -> 0.85 (2026-07-25_loop-test-time-compute) and later to a perfect 1.000 at 5x trained depth (2026-07-26_looped-halt-nrasp). Here it is the WORST arm at every depth: -0.1698 at depths 5-6 and -0.0951 in-distribution versus plain fixed_k4, with NO SEED OVERLAP (per-seed mean of d5/d6 at K=4: fixed 0.611/0.569 vs stochastic 0.490/0.350), and 2-3x the seed spread. What it does buy is exactly what 2026-07-25_filler-vs-recur reported: DEPTH-INVARIANCE, NOT COMPUTE-SCALING - its in-distribution degradation from K=4 to K=8 is only -0.047 against fixed_k4's -0.325. It learned a fixed point whose extra iterations are free of charge AND free of benefit, and paid 0.10-0.17 accuracy for it. (4) DEEP SUPERVISION IS THE CHEAP PRACTICAL WINNER: loss at every iteration matches fixed_k4's in-distribution accuracy (0.6647 vs 0.6651) while inheriting the stochastic arm's robustness (-0.056 at K=8), and is the only arm with a positive - if noise-sized - gain from K>4. (5) THE MODELS ARE NOT JUST RUNNING THE SHORTCUT: against a structure-blind bag-of-digits baseline (apply the ROOT op to every digit in the expression: 1.000/0.550/0.443/0.378/0.344/0.354 at depths 1-6), fixed_k4's margin GROWS with depth: -0.051/+0.050/+0.106/+0.186/+0.227/+0.255. The loop uses structure, and uses it more as trees deepen - it just does not spend a variable number of iterations doing so. (6) PROBE: ITERATION t DOES NOT RESOLVE NESTING LEVEL t. Subtree values are weakly decodable from their ']' latent (0.40 at height 1 vs 0.22 majority; 0.50 at height 6 vs 0.17) but decodability is FLAT in iteration - spread <=0.05 across t=1..8 within every height - and the argmax iteration by height is 5,5,3,2,2,5, with nothing on the t=h diagonal. CAVEATS: (a) ARITY CONFOUND - length is matched but at fixed length depth trades against branching factor (mean max arity 26.7/7.9/5.6/4.8/4.2/3.6 at depth 1-6), so deeper trees here are NARROWER and the flat accuracy-vs-depth curve (fixed_k4 0.949/0.599/0.548/0.564/0.570/0.609) must not be read as 'depth is free'; the K-claims are unaffected because they are within-depth comparisons; (b) UNDERTRAINED - 700 steps, batch 64, ~45k examples, final train loss 0.87-1.42 nats, accuracies 0.42-0.67, and the stochastic arm sees each k a quarter as often, so slower convergence is the largest threat to finding (3); (c) 2 seeds, one width, one op set, one length band, one LR; (d) depth-1 instances are wide flat digit lists (arity ~27) by construction, the price of the length control; (e) fixed_k4 shows a reproducible secondary bump at K=7 (0.447 vs 0.354 at K=6, depth 6), i.e. a period-3-ish orbit rather than convergence - noted, not investigated.

novelty_check.conclusion: PARTIAL-PRIOR-ART, and the closest prior work is a 2026 POSITIVE result that this run fails to reproduce under a control it does not apply. 2603.21676 ('Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization') was fetched and is the direct hit: it trains a depth-recurrent transformer on NESTED BOOLEAN LOGIC at nesting depths 1-8 with the thinking-step count sampled T~U(1,12) - exactly the stochastic-depth recipe tested here - and reports >90% accuracy out to depth 14 with stable behaviour when unrolled to 24 steps. Crucially the fetch confirms it does NOT manipulate sequence length independently of nesting depth ('the nesting depth appears to directly determine the expression complexity and presumably its length, but this distinction isn't independently manipulated'). 2604.07822 ('Loop, Think, & Generalize') shows the same depth extrapolation for recurrent-depth transformers but on multi-hop knowledge-graph chains (serial), analysed with logit-lens rather than per-subtree probes and with no length control. 2402.00976 ('Investigating Recurrent Transformers with Dynamic Halt') evaluates recurrent/universal transformers ON ListOps but as a benchmark score, not as a depth-extrapolation study. The task family is ListOps (Nangia & Bowman, NAACL-SRW 2018) and the backlog's listed prior art is UW-Madison-Lee-Lab/looped-tf. WHAT THIS ROW CONTRIBUTES: (i) the LENGTH-DECOUPLED construction - every expression at every depth grown to the same token band (29.4-29.7 mean tokens at depths 1-6), which none of the above applies, so the published positives cannot separate depth extrapolation from length extrapolation, and once separated here there is no depth extrapolation and no depth-dependent optimal K; (ii) a structure-blind bag-of-digits shortcut floor (apply the root op to all digits) that turns out to be the number that makes ListOps accuracies interpretable and that we could not find used anywhere; (iii) a per-iteration x per-subtree-height decodability matrix as a direct test of 'iteration t resolves level t', refuted; (iv) a same-harness three-way fixed-K vs stochastic-depth vs deep-supervision comparison at exactly matched parameters, steps and batch stream. This is a NEGATIVE against a 2026 positive at 0.136M params on CPU and it is undertrained, so it should be read as 'the recipe did not transfer here, at this scale, under a length control', not as a refutation of 2603.21676.

title: Data repetition at fixed compute, 0.17M params: the '4 epochs is free' knee is at R=1.7 with contiguous subsets - but 90% of that penalty is corpus coverage, not repetition, and the controlled knee is >8.6
hypothesis: Muennighoff et al. (arXiv:2305.16264) find that up to ~4 epochs of repeated data cost almost nothing versus fresh data at 10M-9B params. At ~0.17M params on a ~1M-character corpus - 60x below the smallest model in that paper - the knee should NOT sit at 4 epochs; follow-up work (arXiv:2511.13421) argues the repetition allowance grows with unique-dataset size, so with tiny unique pools the knee was expected EARLIER than 4.
question: At a fixed total-token compute budget and ~0.17M parameters, at what repetition count R = budget_tokens / unique_tokens does val bits-per-character leave a 2% band around the all-fresh (R~1) value, and where does degradation become steep - is the knee near 4 epochs as at 4B+ scale, or elsewhere? And how does the train-val gap (memorization signature) move with R?
method: nanoGPT-style 2-layer pre-norm decoder-only char LM on tiny-shakespeare: d_model=80, 4 heads, d_ff=320, block size 96, learned absolute positions, no biases, untied head, 172,480 params. Every arm has IDENTICAL model shape, identical init at equal seed, identical optimiser and schedule, and an identical FIXED COMPUTE budget of 700 steps x batch 16 x 96 tokens = 1,075,200 tokens. The only thing varied is the amount of UNIQUE data those tokens are drawn from: a contiguous prefix of the train split of fraction u in {1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32}, giving repetition counts R = 1.07, 2.14, 4.28, 8.57, 17.13, 34.32. Split: last 10% of the 1,115,394-char corpus (111,539 chars) is val, fixed and disjoint from every unique subset; headline val bpc on the first 46,080 val chars = 475 non-overlapping 97-char windows, identical windows for every run. Data ordering is TRUE EPOCHING, not random offset sampling: the unique subset is cut into non-overlapping (block+1)-char windows, shuffled with a seeded RNG, consumed, then reshuffled - so R is an exact epoch count. Optimisation held fixed across arms: AdamW lr 3e-3, 70-step warmup, cosine to 10%, betas (0.9,0.95), wd 0.1 on 2-D weights only, grad clip 1.0. Memorization readout: train bpc evaluated on 300 evenly spaced windows drawn from the unique subset the model actually trained on; gap = val bpc - train bpc. CONTROL ARM ('spread'), the piece the naive design needs: at u=1/8 and u=1/32, the SAME number of unique windows is sampled EVENLY ACROSS THE WHOLE train split instead of taken as a prefix - same R, same unique-char count, same compute, only corpus COVERAGE differs. This is needed because a shorter prefix is not only less data, it is also a narrower and textually more distant slice of Shakespeare relative to a val split taken from the END of the corpus. 6 fractions x 2 seeds + 2 control points x 2 seeds = 16 runs.
architecture: 2-layer pre-norm decoder-only transformer, d_model=80, 4 heads (head_dim 20), d_ff=320 GELU, block size 96, learned absolute positions, no biases, untied output head; 172,480 params; identical in every arm

dataset.license: public domain text; char-rnn repo MIT

task: autoregressive character-level language modelling; val bits/character vs data repetition count R at fixed total-token compute

metrics.headline: val bpc vs repetition count R at fixed 1.075M-token compute; the R at which val bpc leaves a 2% band around the all-fresh (R~1) value, with a prefix-vs-spread control isolating corpus coverage from repetition
metrics.epoching: exact: non-overlapping windows shuffled per epoch, not random-offset sampling

result_summary: THE KNEE IS NOWHERE NEAR 4 - and which side of 4 it falls on depends entirely on how the corpus is shrunk. PART 1 (the specified design, contiguous prefixes): at a fixed 1,075,200-token budget, only R=1.07 sits inside the 2% band around the all-fresh val bpc of 3.0658 (band top 3.1271). The very FIRST doubling, R=2.14, already costs +3.10%; R=4.28 costs +7.59%; log-interpolated 2% crossing is R=1.68, i.e. 2.4x BELOW the paper's 4-epoch knee. Seeds are tight (mean spread 0.0260 bpc; total sweep range 1.8193 bpc = 70x the seed spread), so the curve is signal, not noise. Degradation is SMOOTH from R=1 to R=17 (+0.095, +0.138, +0.157, +0.175 bpc per doubling) and then EXPLODES: the 17.1->34.3 doubling alone costs +1.255 bpc, 7.2x the previous doubling and 48x the seed spread. The memorization signature is textbook: train bpc on the unique subset falls monotonically 2.9665 -> 1.9020 while val bpc rises 3.0658 -> 4.8851, and the train-val gap grows 30x, +0.099 -> +2.983 bits. PART 2, THE FINDING THAT MATTERS: the prefix design is confounded, because a shorter prefix is not just less data but a narrower slice of Shakespeare further from a val split taken from the END of the corpus. The spread control holds unique-char count, R and compute fixed while restoring corpus coverage, and at R=8.57 it recovers almost the entire penalty: val bpc 3.1022 (+1.19% over all-fresh, INSIDE the 2% band) versus 3.4552 (+12.70%) for the prefix - 90.6% of the measured repetition penalty is corpus coverage, not repetition, a confound 9x larger than the effect. The train-val gap collapses with it (0.175 spread vs 0.844 prefix), so the 'memorization' at moderate R was largely distribution shift. At R=34.32 the control rescues much less (4.4414, +44.87%, versus 4.8851, +59.34%; only 24.4% coverage), so past ~17 epochs the damage is genuine repetition damage. NET: the coverage-corrected knee is bracketed at 8.6 < R <= 34.3, ABOVE the paper's 4, while the naive prefix measurement lands at 1.7, BELOW it - the two readings bracket 4 from opposite sides and neither lands on it. METHODOLOGICAL UPSHOT: any data-repetition sweep that shrinks the unique pool by taking contiguous subsets will systematically UNDERSTATE the repetition allowance. Our prior (from arXiv:2511.13421, allowance grows with dataset size, so tiny pools should tolerate fewer repeats) is confirmed only by the confounded measurement and refuted by the controlled one. Caveats: (1) EARLY-TRAINING, COMPUTE-POOR regime - all arms sit at 3.0-4.9 bpc against a converged tiny char LM's ~1.5, so this measures fitting speed under repetition rather than a converged loss, and it is the opposite regime from the paper's compute-rich/data-poor one; the tiny model tolerates repeats partly because it has not extracted the pool even once; (2) 2 seeds, one model size, one LR, one corpus; (3) the control was run at only 2 of 6 points, so the corrected knee is bracketed, not localized; (4) character-level Shakespeare is far more redundant than the token-level web text of the source paper.

novelty_check.conclusion: PARTIAL-PRIOR-ART. The 4-epoch claim itself is squarely prior art: Muennighoff et al. (2305.16264, NeurIPS 2023) state verbatim that 'training with up to 4 epochs of repeated data yields negligible changes to loss compared to having unique data', across 'more than 400 models ranging from 10 million to 9 billion parameters' and up to 900B tokens. The key fact the fetch established is that the SMALLEST model in that paper is 10M params - about 60x larger than the 0.17M model here - so the sub-1M regime this row occupies is genuinely untested by the source. Prior art on the scale-dependence question also exists and is recent: 'Larger Datasets Can Be Repeated More' (2511.13421) argues directly against a universal 4-epoch constant, showing the effective reuse rate E(K,N) saturates at a point that GROWS with unique-dataset size N (Theta(log N) under strong convexity, a power of N under power-law data distributions) and concluding 'larger datasets can be repeated more times before the marginal benefit vanishes'. That paper supplies the prior this experiment set out to test, and it is a prior about DATASET size, not model size. Also adjacent: 'To Repeat or Not To Repeat' (2305.13230) and Anthropic's 'scaling laws and interpretability of learning from repeated data', both at >=100M scale. WHAT THIS ROW ADDS AND THE SEARCH DID NOT SURFACE: (a) the repetition sweep run at 0.17M params, ~60x below the smallest published point, CPU-only in under 10 minutes, with exact epoch semantics rather than random-offset sampling; (b) the PREFIX-VS-SPREAD CONTROL, which decomposes the measured repetition penalty into a corpus-coverage component and a true-repetition component (90.6% / 9.4% at R=8.6) - we could not find this control published anywhere, and it inverts which side of 4 the answer falls on, which makes it a methodological warning for every small-scale repetition sweep that shrinks its pool contiguously; (c) the train-val gap reported per repetition level as an explicit memorization readout, and shown to be itself largely a coverage artefact at moderate R. The 'no published version of this control' claim is a negative search result over web and paper search, not an exhaustive literature review; arXiv and OpenAlex APIs 403 from this environment, so the verdict rests on 2 web searches plus 3 direct page fetches.
