title: Clock vs pizza on (a+b) mod 59: the attention-rate knob moves the model between the two published archetypes, but the field's two discriminators disagree by 2x about where the phase boundary is (r*=0.43-0.60 by gradient symmetricity, 0.84 by distance irrelevance)
hypothesis: Zhong et al. (arXiv:2306.17844) show a 1-layer transformer on (a+b) mod p implements either the 'clock' algorithm (attention multiplies rotations; the correct logit is independent of a-b) or the 'pizza' algorithm (operand embeddings are averaged, so the correct logit picks up an amplitude factor cos(pi*w*(a-b)/p)), and that the choice is set by an 'attention rate' alpha interpolating attention toward a constant matrix. Interpolating attention toward uniform with rate r = 1 - alpha should therefore drive the model from clock to pizza, and the paper's two discriminators - gradient symmetricity s_g (Def 4.1) and distance irrelevance q (Def 4.2) - should both move monotonically in r and locate the SAME phase boundary.
question: As the attention matrix of a 1-layer modular-addition transformer is interpolated toward uniform, att = (1-r)*softmax + r*(1/T), where does the clock->pizza phase boundary sit, is the crossover sharp or gradual, and do the two canonical discriminators agree about its location - all while every arm still solves the task?
method: 1-layer LayerNorm-free, bias-free transformer over [a, b, '='], logits read from the last position only, on all 59^2 = 3481 pairs of (a+b) mod 59 with a deterministic random 50/50 split. p=59 is the paper's own modulus and is NOT shrunk; d_model=64 (the paper fixes width 128 for its attention-rate figure and sweeps 32-512 elsewhere), 4 heads, d_mlp=128, 40,576 params. Full-batch AdamW, lr 1e-3, weight decay 1.0, betas (0.9, 0.98), init std 0.8/sqrt(d) - the recipe already validated by the sibling rows 2026-07-25_grokking-modular-addition and 2026-07-25_grokking-weight-decay-phase. THE KNOB: att = (1-r)*softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_head)) + r*(1/T), with r the uniform-attention mixing rate; r=0 is a standard transformer (the paper's alpha=1, predicted clock) and r=1 is constant attention (the paper's alpha=0, their 'Model A', predicted pizza); alpha = 1-r is reported alongside. We keep attention rows stochastic rather than using the paper's all-ONE matrix J, which is the same family up to a constant row scale the learnable W_O absorbs. ARMS: r in {0, 0.25, 0.375, 0.5, 0.625, 0.75, 1.0} x 2 seeds = 14 runs, all of which fit the budget (0 skipped); r=0.375 and 0.625 are boundary-refinement points. FAIRNESS: at equal seed every arm gets the IDENTICAL initialisation, the IDENTICAL data split and the IDENTICAL 1200 optimiser steps - 1200 is well past every arm's grokking point (600-950 steps), so all arms are read in the same grokked-and-consolidated state rather than at whatever step each happened to converge. DISCRIMINATORS, implemented verbatim from the paper: (1) gradient symmetricity s_g = mean over 400 random (a,b,c) triples of cos(dQ_abc/dE_a, dQ_abc/dE_b), with c sampled uniformly and NOT required to be the correct answer - under uniform attention the last-position stream depends on the operands only through (E_a+E_b)W_V/T, making the network an exactly symmetric function of the two embeddings, so s_g -> 1; (2) distance irrelevance q = mean_d std_i(L[i, i+d]) / std(L) on the correct-logit matrix L[i,j] = Q_{ij,i+j}, which holds the distance d = b-a fixed and asks how much the correct logit still varies as the SUM sweeps, so pizza -> 0 and clock -> 1. The paper's own reported values (pizza s_g 0.9937 / q 0.17; clock s_g 0.3336 / q 0.85, with bands pizza q in [0,0.4] and clock q in [0.4,1]) are used as FIXED reference thresholds, not fitted. Boundaries are located by linear interpolation of the seed-mean curves at two thresholds each: the sweep's own r=0/r=1 endpoint midpoint, and the paper-referenced threshold. VALIDITY CONTROL, the piece the naive design needs: mixing attention toward uniform makes the network a more symmetric function of its operands whether or not it has learned anything, so both discriminators are ALSO measured on the UNTRAINED model at the same r and seed, before a single gradient step, to separate an architectural ramp from a learned one. Supporting readouts: scale-free amplitude of the correct-logit distance modulation, embedding Fourier effective-frequency count (an algorithm-agnostic check that every arm learned a sparse Fourier solution), and realised attention L1 deviation from uniform (a check that the knob acts as intended).
architecture: 1-layer attention + ReLU MLP transformer, no LayerNorm, no biases; d_model=64, 4 heads (head_dim 16), d_mlp=128, n_ctx=3 ([a, b, '=']), vocab p+1=60, untied unembedding; 40,576 params; attention distribution interpolated toward uniform at rate r

dataset.name: all 59^2 = 3481 (a, b) pairs for (a+b) mod 59; one deterministic random 50/50 split per seed (1740 train / 1741 test)
dataset.source: generated in run.py from the seed

task: modular addition (a+b) mod 59; algorithm identification (clock vs pizza) as a function of the uniform-attention mixing rate r
compute: CPU 1 thread, 606s (10.1 min) for 14 training runs + discriminator evaluation + untrained-init control

metrics.headline: distance irrelevance q and gradient symmetricity s_g (Zhong et al. Defs 4.2 / 4.1) vs the uniform-attention mixing rate r, with the clock->pizza phase boundary located by linear interpolation, plus test accuracy per r
metrics.censored_detail: r=0.375 seed 1 reached train acc 1.0 but test acc 0.9443, just under the 0.95 grok threshold; its r=0.375 row is a mean over one grokked and one marginal run

result_summary: THE KNOB WORKS, THE ENDPOINTS REPRODUCE THE PAPER, AND THE TWO CANONICAL DISCRIMINATORS THEN DISAGREE BY 2x ABOUT WHERE THE BOUNDARY IS. Interpolating attention toward uniform does carry a 1-layer transformer between the two published archetypes: at r=0 (standard attention) distance irrelevance is q=0.854, essentially the paper's clock value of 0.85, with gradient symmetricity s_g=-0.156, i.e. MORE clock-like than their clock model's 0.3336; at r=1 (constant attention) s_g=1.000 against their pizza's 0.9937. But the two metrics then locate the transition in different places. Gradient symmetricity rises monotonically across all SEVEN r values (-0.156, 0.027, 0.343, 0.521, 0.708, 0.841, 1.000) and crosses its own endpoint midpoint at r*=0.431 (alpha*=0.569) and the paper-referenced threshold 0.664 at r*=0.596 (alpha*=0.404). Distance irrelevance is NOT monotone (0.854, 0.874, 0.852, 0.875, 0.820, 0.780, 0.521), stays clock-like until r=0.75, crosses its own midpoint only at r*=0.840 (alpha*=0.160), and NEVER reaches the paper's pizza ceiling of q<=0.4 - even the fully-uniform-attention arm sits at q=0.521, so under the paper's own classification bands our maximally-pizza model would still be labelled CLOCK. SIGNAL-TO-NOISE IS THE DECIDING FACT: s_g swings 1.156 end-to-end against a worst seed spread of 0.134 (SNR 8.6), while q swings only 0.333 against a worst seed spread of 0.207 (SNR 1.6) - barely above the run-to-run noise floor, and at r=1 the two seeds give q=0.417 and q=0.625, one inside the paper's pizza band and one nowhere near it. So at this width s_g is the usable discriminator and q is not. SHAPE: the crossover is GRADUAL for s_g (sharpness ratio 1.64, i.e. nearly a straight ramp, not the sharp phase transition the paper describes) and ABRUPT for q (3.72, its entire movement concentrated in the final r: 0.75->1.0 interval). The mechanistic reading is that the metrics come apart because they measure different things: s_g probes the COMPUTATIONAL GRAPH (does the network treat its two operands symmetrically?) and moves smoothly and early, while q probes BEHAVIOUR (does the answer logit depend on b-a?) and only fires once the model is almost entirely attention-free - a model can be structurally symmetric long before that symmetry surfaces as distance-dependent logits. THE CONTROL THAT LICENSES THE s_g READING: because mixing attention toward uniform mechanically symmetrises the network, both metrics were also measured on the UNTRAINED model at each r. The untrained baseline is FLAT - s_g in [0.9998, 1.0] and q = 0.9994 at every r including r=0, because at initialisation the QK weights are small enough that softmax is already near-uniform - so the init swing is 0.0002 versus the trained swing of 1.156, a ratio of 5781x. None of the measured ramp is an artefact of the knob; training is what drives s_g down to -0.156 at r=0, i.e. low-r models LEARN to break the operand symmetry. Honest counter-caveat: s_g=1.000 exactly at r=1 IS architecturally forced (uniform attention makes the network a literally symmetric function of E_a and E_b), so that single endpoint is not evidence - the interior of the curve is. CONTROLS PASS: every arm reached train accuracy 1.000 and 13/14 reached test accuracy >=0.95, so the sweep compares algorithms rather than competence; the embedding effective-frequency count stays at 5.1-6.1 across all r, so every arm learned a sparse Fourier solution; realised attention L1 deviation from uniform falls monotonically 0.936 -> 0.000, confirming the knob acts as intended. ONE CENSORED ARM: r=0.375 seed 1 finished at test accuracy 0.9443, just under the 0.95 threshold, so that r's row mixes one grokked and one marginal run. NET: 'cannot cleanly locate a single phase boundary at this scale and budget' - the endpoints are cleanly discriminated, the boundary is not, and the disagreement between the field's two standard metrics (r*=0.43-0.60 vs 0.84 on identical runs) is itself the finding. Caveats: (1) width 64 with 2 seeds, versus the paper's width 128 and alpha sampled uniformly over [0,1] - the paper explicitly reports that the phase-change point MOVES with width, so r* here is not expected to match theirs numerically; (2) 1200 steps is past grokking but far from converged, and weight decay keeps reshaping the solution, so q may be measured on a still-drifting logit scale; (3) the interpolation keeps attention rows stochastic rather than using the paper's all-one matrix J; (4) two seeds cannot distinguish q's bimodality at r=1 from genuine algorithmic bistability.

novelty_check.conclusion: REPLICATION. This is not adjacent prior art - it is the same experiment. Zhong, Liu, Andreas & Tegmark, 'The Clock and the Pizza' (arXiv:2306.17844, NeurIPS 2023) define the attention-rate interpolation M' = M*alpha + J*(1-alpha), define both discriminators used here (Definition 4.1 gradient symmetricity s_g = mean cos(dQ_abc/dE_a, dQ_abc/dE_b); Definition 4.2 distance irrelevance q = mean_d std(L_{i,i+d}) / std(L)), sample alpha uniformly in [0,1], and report 'a clear phase transition from the Pizza algorithm to the Clock algorithm' with 'an almost linear phase boundary with regards to both attention rate and layer width'. They use p=59, the same modulus used here, and report pizza s_g 0.9937 / q 0.17 and clock s_g 0.3336 / q 0.85 - values this run consumes as fixed reference thresholds rather than fitting. Both discriminators are therefore reimplemented, not invented. Also checked and adjacent but not duplicative: 'Algorithmic Capabilities of Random Transformers' (arXiv:2410.04368, same first author, reuses these metrics on frozen-embedding models) and 'Algorithmic Phase Transitions in Language Models' (arXiv:2412.07386). Registry siblings 2026-07-25_grokking-modular-addition, 2026-07-25_grokking-weight-decay-phase and 2026-07-25_sae-on-grokked-model share the task and training recipe but none touched clock-vs-pizza. WHAT THIS ROW ADDS ON TOP OF THE REPLICATION: (a) a ~40k-param, 10.7-minute, CPU-only reproduction at width 64, about half the width of the paper's attention-rate figure, showing the endpoint archetypes survive that shrink; (b) both discriminators reported on the SAME r axis WITH a per-r seed-spread noise floor, which is what surfaces their 2x disagreement about r* (0.43-0.60 vs 0.84) and q's signal-to-noise of only 1.6 - the paper reports the metrics but these searches did not surface a published head-to-head boundary comparison or a noise floor for them; (c) the untrained-initialisation control for both metrics (init swing 0.0002 vs trained swing 1.156), which we did not find in the paper and which is what licenses reading the s_g ramp as learned rather than as a mechanical consequence of the knob. The 'not in the paper' claims are negative results from three web searches plus two full-text fetches, not an exhaustive reading of the appendices; arXiv and OpenAlex APIs 403 from this environment.

title: Is Delta-selectivity the load-bearing part of Mamba? At 60k params on selective copy it buys NOTHING (-0.061 token acc vs an LTI baseline at k=4, +0.030 at k=8 inside its own 0.073 seed spread) while input-dependent B/C buys +0.144/+0.109 and the depthwise conv alone beats all selectivity combined - Mamba's own Table-7 ranking inverts on the task the paper invented to motivate selectivity
hypothesis: Mamba (arXiv:2312.00752) motivates input-dependent state updates with the selective-copy task and its own Table 7 (350M params, LM perplexity) names the step size Delta 'the most important parameter'. But Delta is a function of the CURRENT INPUT ONLY - it cannot see the hidden state - which is exactly the property our 2026-07-25_minrnn-selcopy row showed costs minGRU the ORDERING of stored items (per-slot accuracy collapses to the last ~2). Either (a) Delta-selectivity hits the same ordering wall and full Mamba's advantage must come from input-dependent B/C (which route content into specific state dimensions) plus the depthwise conv, or (b) the SSM's structured N-dimensional state, whose per-(channel,state) decay rates exp(Delta*A) form a spectrum of timescales rather than a single leak rate, encodes order as a multi-timescale trace and escapes the wall. We predicted (b) partially: Delta-only beating a fully LTI S4-lite baseline and beating minGRU's recency profile, while still losing to a GRU whose gates see the state.
question: At matched total parameters on selective copy, which component of Mamba's selectivity - the input-dependent step size Delta, or the input-dependent B and C - is load-bearing? Does Delta-selectivity reproduce the ordering failure that an input-only gate (minGRU) shows, and does a full selective SSM beat a GRU where minGRU failed?
method: Hand-rolled minimal Mamba-style (S6) block in pure PyTorch, sequential scan, CPU only - no mamba.py, no state-spaces/mamba, no CUDA kernels. h_t = exp(dt_t*A) . h_{t-1} + (dt_t*B_t) . x_t per (channel,state) pair; y_t = sum_N (h_t . C_t) + D . x_t. d_inner = 2*d_model, N=8 states/channel, diagonal real A = -exp(A_log) with S4D-real init, Mamba's log-uniform dt-bias init, depthwise causal conv width 4, SiLU gating by z, pre-LN residual block, shared GELU bottleneck(64) -> k linear slot heads on the LAST position. FIVE ARMS differing ONLY in which of {dt,B,C} is a function of the current input, with embedding/conv/gate/readout/optimiser/data/seed byte-identical: full (dt,B,C selective = Mamba S6), delta (dt selective; B,C learned constants), bc (B,C selective; dt a learned constant), lti (nothing selective = S4-lite), gru (nn.GRU reference whose gates see x AND h). Each arm's d_model is fitted so TOTAL params ~= 60k (58,674-60,852 across all arms; the LTI arm gets the LARGEST state, so the design is conservative against the claim). TASK AND GENERATOR REUSED VERBATIM from 2026-07-25_minrnn-selcopy for cross-row comparability: length-L sequence of a blank token (id 0) with k data tokens (ids 1..8) at uniformly random positions, target = the k values in order of appearance; core cells L=32 x k in {4,8}, span control at L=64 k=4; fresh data every step, eval on 1024 held-out sequences from a disjoint seed (binomial SE ~0.016). Held fixed: 600 steps, batch 32, AdamW lr 8e-3 (OneCycle, 10% warmup), grad clip 1.0, weight decay 0.01 on 2-D weights ONLY - never on A_log, D, dt bias or norms, since decaying A_log would itself be an ablation. LR IS NOT A CONFOUND: a documented pre-sweep (metrics.lr_pre_sweep) ran all five arms at lr in {3e-3, 8e-3} and 8e-3 is best or tied-best for EVERY arm. CONTROLS/PROBES: full_noconv (depthwise conv removed, measured on the same scale as the selectivity terms); seed 1 for all five arms at L=32 k=8; span control at L=64 k=4; a 2-block delta depth probe. MECHANISM READOUTS: per-slot accuracy and a recency index (mean of last 2 slots minus mean of the rest, +1 = only the last two items readable) as the ordering measure; a retention spectrum reading exp(dt*A) per (channel,state) while the model idles on blank tokens, reported as median retention, median half-life in tokens, and the fraction of states with half-life > L; and mean dt on noise vs data tokens as the Mamba analogue of minGRU's input-gate statistic. 21 runs.
architecture: hand-rolled minimal Mamba/S6 selective SSM, 1 block (2 for the depth probe), d_model 84-88, d_inner = 2*d_model, N=8 states/channel, depthwise causal conv width 4, SiLU gating, pre-LN residual; ~60k params in every arm; nn.GRU reference at matched params (d_model 50-52, hidden 100-104)

result_summary: THE MAMBA PAPER'S OWN SELECTIVITY RANKING INVERTS ON THE TASK IT INVENTED TO MOTIVATE SELECTIVITY. At 60k matched params on selective copy, decomposing against an LTI (nothing-selective) baseline: dt-only selectivity is worth -0.046 exact / -0.061 per-token at k=4 and +0.030 per-token at k=8 - a gain smaller than dt's OWN seed spread of 0.073, i.e. indistinguishable from zero - while B,C-only selectivity is worth +0.194 exact / +0.144 token at k=4 and +0.109 token at k=8 (9x the arm spreads). Full selectivity gives +0.318/+0.201. Mamba Table 7 (350M, Pile perplexity) reports the opposite ordering: dt-only recovers 1.12 of the 2.22 ppl that full selectivity gains, more than B-only (0.78) or C-only (0.95), and the paper states verbatim 'Delta is the most important parameter (Theorem 1)'. THE DEPTHWISE CONV BEATS ALL OF IT: removing it takes the full arm from 0.381 to 0.036 exact at k=4 (+0.228 per-token, versus +0.201 for all three selectivity mechanisms combined). MECHANISM 1 - dt IS LEARNED, AND THE LEARNING IS WHAT HURTS: reading the retention exp(dt*A) per (channel,state) while the model idles on blanks, the dt-only arm has median retention 0.700 / median half-life 1.95 tokens and only 13.4% of states with half-life > L, against the LTI baseline's 0.950 / 13.5 tokens / 31.0% and the full arm's 0.968 / 21.2 / 41.5%. Because Abar = exp(dt*A) with A<0, an input-dependent dt is a knob the optimiser pushes UP, so it buys a gate and pays with its memory - median half-life collapses 14 -> 2 tokens. Corroborating this, the arm with the MOST extreme learned dt-selectivity (full_noconv, dt ratio 38.8x data-over-noise) is one of the WORST performers (0.036), while the best SSM arm has a ratio of only 1.6x. MECHANISM 2 - dt HITS THE SAME ORDERING WALL AS minGRU, HARDER: per-slot accuracy at L=32 k=8 (chance 0.125) for the dt-only arm is [0.14, 0.14, 0.19, 0.21, 0.24, 0.27, 0.75, 1.00] - the last two items perfect, the first four at the chance floor - recency index 0.675, worse than minGRU's 0.375 in registry row 2026-07-25_minrnn-selcopy. The B,C-selective arm is the flattest SSM ([0.40, 0.37, 0.38, 0.38, 0.37, 0.43, 0.56, 0.95], recency 0.371, on par with the GRU's 0.367) and lifts slot 1 from 0.14 to 0.40. So the structured N-dimensional state does NOT rescue an input-only gate; the answer is the pessimistic branch. The split is mechanistically clean: dt is a scalar 'how fast do I forget right now' leak rate - exactly minGRU's z - whereas B is 'which state dimensions does this token write into', an ADDRESS, and ordering needs an address. NOBODY BEATS THE GRU: full Mamba reaches 0.381 exact at k=4 against the GRU's 1.000, and against minGRU's 0.389 at the same 60k params and 600 steps - so full Mamba does not even beat minGRU here; at k=8 the GRU is the only arm with non-trivial exact match (0.032) and leads on per-token accuracy 0.700 vs 0.497. PROBES: a 2-block dt-only model at the same params goes 0.017 -> 0.065 exact with slot 3 jumping 0.47 -> 0.995, so depth partially substitutes for the missing state-dependent gate (the same substitution the minGRU row found); the L=64 k=4 span control flips the SSM ranking (delta 0.085 > full 0.023) on a single seed and is read as instability, with the GRU still at 1.000. CAVEATS: 600 steps, 60k params (Mamba's ablation: 350M), 1 block, N=8, L<=64 (paper: 4096), vocab 8, 2 seeds at k=8 and 1 elsewhere; at k=8 exact match is on the floor for every SSM arm so that column rests on per-token accuracy; the lr was fixed at 8e-3 by a documented pre-sweep in which 8e-3 was best or tied-best for every one of the five arms, so it favours nobody; our bc arm turns B AND C on together whereas Table 7 reports them singly; and the contradicted ablation was measured on language-modelling perplexity, where aggressive forgetting is a feature and per-item ordering is never scored, so both findings can be true at once. The defensible claim is the negative one: at this scale dt-selectivity buys nothing measurable on selective copy, while B/C-selectivity and the depthwise conv each buy a lot.

novelty_check.conclusion: PARTIAL-PRIOR-ART. The ablation AXIS is squarely prior art and we found its exact numbers: Mamba (arXiv:2312.00752) Table 7, ~350M params on language-modelling perplexity, reports nothing-selective 10.93, B-only 10.15, C-only 9.98, Delta-only 9.81, all-three 8.71, and concludes verbatim 'Delta is the most important parameter (Theorem 1), but using multiple selective parameters together synergizes'. Its Table 1 reports selective copying (S6 97.0-99.8 vs S4 18.3) but there selectivity is ALL-OR-NOTHING - the per-parameter Delta/B/C ablation is never run on selective copy, only on perplexity. That gap is what this row fills, and the ranking inverts inside it. The other close paper, 'Understanding Input Selectivity in Mamba' (arXiv:2506.11891, ICML 2025), analyses a 'simplified S6 where the input-dependence only affects the state matrix via Delta(x)' and reports that a 1-layer Mamba can solve MQAR exactly WITHOUT input-dependence in its SSM, stressing 'the importance of convolution and gating' - which independently corroborates our conv-control finding - but it is theory-plus-MQAR and does not run a controlled matched-parameter Delta-vs-B/C accuracy ablation on selective copy. WHAT THIS ROW ADDS AND THE SEARCH DID NOT SURFACE: (a) the Delta/B/C ablation run on SELECTIVE COPY at matched total parameters, with the ranking inverted relative to Table 7; (b) a per-slot ORDERING readout (recency index) that connects the result to a previously isolated failure mode of input-only gates from our own registry (2026-07-25_minrnn-selcopy), showing Delta-only reproduces minGRU's recency signature MORE extremely (0.675 vs 0.375) than minGRU does; (c) a mechanism - the retention-spectrum measurement showing input-dependent Delta SHORTENS median memory half-life from ~14 to ~2 tokens, i.e. the gate is learned and the learning is what costs the ordering; (d) the depthwise conv quantified on the SAME scale as the selectivity terms, where it exceeds all of them combined at k=4; (e) a matched-parameter GRU reference, which neither the Mamba nor the minRNN paper runs on this task. The 'no published version of this specific ablation' claim is a negative search result over 4 web searches plus 3 direct paper fetches, not an exhaustive literature review; arXiv/OpenAlex APIs 403 from this environment.

title: Is the closed-form continuous-time (CfC/liquid) cell more robust to UNSEEN sampling irregularity than a GRU that just gets dt as an input? No - at 20k matched params on irregularly-sampled sine mixtures and Mackey-Glass the two are indistinguishable (gap inside seed spread at the trained level, and the sign of the gap FLIPS between datasets at 4x interval variance), while a CfC whose gate is fed a constant dt lands exactly on the dt-blind GRU: the entire advantage is the dt channel, none of it is the closed form
hypothesis: A hand-rolled CfC cell (Hasani et al. arXiv:2106.13898 Eq. 10), whose state-mixing coefficient c = sigmoid(-f(x,h)*dt + b) is a closed-form function of the elapsed time, should degrade gracefully when the test sampling irregularity is 2-4x more variable than anything seen in training, while a dt-blind GRU collapses. The honest question under test is whether the cheap fix - appending dt as an extra input feature to a matched-parameter GRU - already closes that gap; an 'dt-as-input matches CfC' outcome is a fully successful result.
question: At matched parameters on next-value prediction from irregularly-sampled continuous-time signals, how much of the CfC's advantage over recurrent baselines is the closed-form continuous-time gate and how much is merely having the elapsed time somewhere in the model? Does the CfC generalize better than a dt-as-input GRU to irregularity levels never seen in training (2x and 4x interval variance), and to the reverse shift (perfectly regular sampling)?
method: Hand-rolled CfC cell in pure PyTorch - no ncps, no raminmh/CfC clone, no CUDA. Implements arXiv:2106.13898 Eq. (10) x(t) = sigma(-f(x,I;theta_f) t) . g(x,I;theta_g) + (1 - sigma(-[f(x,I;theta_f)] t)) . h(x,I;theta_h) in the parametrisation of the official CfCCell: a shared tanh backbone over z=[input;state] feeding four linear heads ff1(=h), ff2(=g), time_a(=-f), time_b, with c = sigmoid(time_a(z)*dt + time_b(z)) and state' = (1-c)*ff1(z) + c*ff2(z); time_b is the reference implementation's elapsed-time-independent bias (absent from Eq. 10 as printed, without which c is pinned to 0.5 at dt=0). The mixing coefficient is the ONLY place dt enters. FIVE ARMS at matched total parameters (20001-20287, +-0.7%), differing ONLY in how dt reaches the state: cfc (closed-form gate, hidden 63); gru_dt (dt concatenated to the input - the cheap fix under test, hidden 80); decay_gru (GRU-D-style per-unit exponential state decay h <- h*exp(-dt*softplus(w)) before the GRU update, hidden 80); gru_blind (dt never seen, hidden 80); and cfc_fixed_dt, a CONTROL with the identical CfC architecture whose gate always sees dt = mu, which separates 'the CfC architecture' from 'the CfC uses dt'. Every arm runs the identical recurrence h_{i+1} = Cell(x_i, h_i, dt_i) with dt_i = t_{i+1} - t_i and yhat_{i+1} = W h_{i+1} + b predicting x_{i+1}, so dt_i is SIMULTANEOUSLY the elapsed time of the state update and the forecast horizon - the task is well posed for a model that sees dt and under-determined for one that does not, which is the property under test. TWO SIGNAL FAMILIES, both continuous-time and both sampled at arbitrary real times: (a) sine mixtures x(t) = sum_{k=1,2} a_k sin(2 pi f_k t + phi_k), per-sequence random a~U(0.5,1.5), f~U(0.03,0.20), phi~U(0,2pi), variance normalised to 1, so each sequence is a different function the model must identify in context; (b) Mackey-Glass tau=17 using the RK4 integrator reused from 2026-07-25_esn-reservoir but kept DENSE (grid 0.05, no subsampling) and linearly interpolated at the irregular sample times, tanh(x-1)-squashed then standardised, sequences = random windows of one 3300-time-unit trajectory. IRREGULARITY SWEEP: intervals ~ Gamma(k=1/cv^2, scale=mu/k), giving mean EXACTLY mu=1 and coefficient of variation EXACTLY cv, nothing clipped. Trained at cv=0.6 ONLY; evaluated at cv in {0.0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.8485, 1.2} = regular / half-variance / trained / 2x interval variance / 4x interval variance. The MEAN interval is pinned in every regime so the average forecast horizon never changes and the shift is pure sampling-variance, tested in both directions. The eval set holds the UNDERLYING SIGNALS FIXED across regimes (512 sequences, same a,f,phi and same MG windows) - only the sampling grid changes. HELD FIXED: 700 steps, batch 48, sequence length 48, burn-in 8 (first 8 predictions excluded from loss and metrics), AdamW + cosine schedule with 10% warmup, wd 0.01 on 2-D weights only, grad clip 1.0, 2 seeds per (arm, dataset), fresh data every step, eval on 512 held-out sequences from a disjoint generator seed. Every arm sees byte-identical training batches (the data generator is seeded by (dataset, seed) only). LR IS NOT A CONFOUND: a documented 15-run pre-sweep over lr in {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2} (metrics.lr_pre_sweep_mse_at_train_cv) selected 1e-2 for ALL FIVE arms, so every arm runs at its own grid-best lr. Reference scales reported on the identical eval batches: persistence (predict x_i) and target variance. 35 runs (15 pre-sweep + 20 headline).
architecture: hand-rolled CfC cell (arXiv:2106.13898 Eq. 10, ncps CfCCell parametrisation) at hidden 63 / 20287 params, vs nn.GRU and nn.GRUCell baselines at hidden 80 / 20001-20241 params; iso-parameter within +-0.7%; single recurrent layer + linear readout in every arm

dataset.name: synthetic irregularly-sampled continuous-time signals: (a) random 2-component sine mixtures, (b) Mackey-Glass tau=17
dataset.source: generated in run.py (analytic sines; RK4 Mackey-Glass on a dense dt=0.05 grid, linearly interpolated at the irregular sample times; MG integrator reused from experiments/2026-07-25_esn-reservoir/run.py). Train generator seeded by (dataset, seed); eval signals from a disjoint seed.

task: next-value prediction from irregular samples: given (x_i, dt_i) predict x at t_i + dt_i; headline = MSE per arm at four sampling-irregularity regimes (regular / trained / 2x interval variance / 4x interval variance) with the mean interval pinned
compute: CPU 1 thread, 675s (11.25 min) for 35 runs (15 lr pre-sweep + 20 headline) including all evaluation

metrics.headline: next-value MSE per arm at four sampling-irregularity regimes (regular / trained / 2x interval variance / 4x interval variance) at matched ~50k params; mean interval identical in every regime

result_summary: HYPOTHESIS HALF-CONFIRMED, HALF-REFUTED - and the refuted half is the interesting one. (1) THE dt-BLIND GRU DOES COLLAPSE: at the trained irregularity (cv=0.6) it is 13.3x worse than the CfC on sine mixtures (0.2821 vs 0.02116 MSE) and 11.1x worse on Mackey-Glass (0.00974 vs 0.00088), on both datasets and both seeds. (2) BUT dt-AS-INPUT FULLY CLOSES THE GAP, AND THE RESIDUAL GAP CHANGES SIGN BETWEEN DATASETS. At the trained level CfC minus GRU+dt is -0.00024 (sine) and -0.00020 (MG), both inside the GRU+dt seed spread (0.00162 / 0.00017). Under the UNSEEN regimes: at 2x interval variance the CfC wins 8.7% on sine (per-seed 0.0647/0.0649 vs 0.0710/0.0708, non-overlapping) and ties on MG (+0.5%); at 4x interval variance the CfC wins 1.6% on sine (inside spread) and LOSES 33% on MG (0.01059 vs 0.00799; per-seed 0.0102/0.0110 vs 0.0071/0.0088, non-overlapping). A 20k-param GRU with one extra input scalar is as robust to unseen sampling irregularity as the closed-form continuous-time cell. (3) THE FROZEN-dt CONTROL PINS THE MECHANISM: an identical CfC whose gate is always fed dt = mu scores 0.28735 against the dt-blind GRU's 0.28210 on sine (ratio 1.019) and 0.00944 vs 0.00974 on MG (ratio 0.970) - i.e. it lands ON the dt-blind GRU. The backbone, the two tanh heads and the multiplicative interpolation are worth NOTHING; 100% of the CfC's advantage is the elapsed time entering the mixing coefficient. (4) GRU-D-STYLE DECAY IS A COARSE BUT REAL CONTINUOUS-TIME CHANNEL: decay-GRU is 1.6x (sine) / 2.8x (MG) worse than the CfC at the trained level but only 1.11x / 1.37x worse at 4x variance, so a single scalar leak rate per unit recovers most of the benefit. (5) THE 'GRACEFUL DEGRADATION' RATIO IS A TRAP THAT INVERTS THE RANKING: MSE(cv=1.2)/MSE(cv=0.6) makes the dt-blind GRU look like the MOST robust arm (1.78 sine, 3.52 MG) and the CfC the LEAST (7.41, 12.04), purely because the dt-blind arms start from an ~11x worse floor and saturate against the persistence/variance ceiling; in ABSOLUTE MSE the dt-aware arms win every single cell of the sweep. Any robustness claim read off relative degradation alone comes out backwards. (6) THE REVERSE SHIFT DOES NOT RESCUE THE dt-BLIND MODEL: at perfectly regular sampling (cv=0), where dt carries no information at all, the dt-blind GRU is still 21.1x (sine) / 3.9x (MG) worse than the CfC - training under horizon uncertainty without the horizon damages what is learned and the damage does not heal when the test grid becomes regular. Every arm beats persistence everywhere (CfC ~31x better than persistence at the trained level on sine, ~32x on MG, still 4.1x / 4.5x at 4x variance). CAVEATS: 700 steps, 20k params, 2 seeds, length-48 UNIVARIATE fully-observed sequences - none of the multivariate missingness/masking structure GRU-D and the CfC were designed for, where a richer time-aware state may still separate from one appended scalar; the lr grid's winner (1e-2) was at the grid edge for every arm; only the CfC's default interpolation mode was tested, not the gated variant or the full LTC/NCP wiring; and the shift is a pure interval-VARIANCE shift with the mean pinned, not a mean-interval shift.

novelty_check.conclusion: PARTIAL-PRIOR-ART. The comparison AXIS is well-colonised. The CfC paper itself (arXiv:2106.13898 / Nature Machine Intelligence 2022; Eq. 10 is the equation implemented verbatim here) benchmarks against LSTM/GRU/GRU-D/Phased-LSTM/ODE-RNN/CT-GRU/CT-LSTM, and 'Still Competitive: Revisiting Recurrent Models for Irregular Time Series Prediction' (arXiv:2510.16161) makes exactly our headline claim at scale - that simple time-aware GRUs (GRU-Delta-t, GRU-D, their GRUwE) match or beat Neural-ODE, CRU, ContiFormer and transformer models on USHCN/PhysioNet/MIMIC-III at far lower cost - so our 'dt-as-input matches CfC' finding should be read as an independent tiny-CPU corroboration of a claim already in the literature, not as new. WHAT THE SEARCH DID NOT SURFACE, verified by direct fetch of BOTH papers: neither evaluates generalization to an irregularity level DIFFERENT from the training one - the CfC paper uses datasets with inherent irregularity and 2510.16161 uses fixed splits; both fetches state this explicitly. WHAT THIS ROW ADDS: (a) a controlled sampling-irregularity distribution shift with the mean interval pinned so only the variance moves, evaluated in BOTH directions (2x and 4x more irregular, and fully regular), which is the axis the backlog item asked about and neither paper tests; (b) a frozen-dt CfC control that isolates the closed-form architecture from the dt channel and shows the architecture contributes nothing measurable (ratio 1.019 / 0.970 against the dt-blind GRU); (c) strict iso-parameter matching at 20k params with a documented per-arm lr pre-sweep; (d) the explicit demonstration that the relative-degradation metric inverts the robustness ranking, so 'degrades gracefully' must be argued in absolute error. The 'not previously published' claim is a negative search result over 3 web searches plus 2 direct paper fetches, not an exhaustive literature review; arXiv/OpenAlex APIs 403 from this environment.

title: Does Muon's win survive per WALL-CLOCK SECOND on CPU? REFUTED - at 0.42M params and 1024 tokens/step, where Keller's own overhead rule predicts a 62.5% tax instead of the speedrun's 0.73%, the MEASURED tax is only 27.7% while Muon's step-domain speedup is 1.85x, so Muon still wins by 0.274 bpc at matched seconds (1.49x wall-clock speedup); the danger zone is BELOW this batch size, not above it, and a naive bfloat16 Newton-Schulz port would alone have flipped the verdict
hypothesis: Muon's per-step win over AdamW survives at tiny scale, but shrinks or reverses per WALL-CLOCK SECOND on CPU, because the 5-iteration Newton-Schulz orthogonalization is a FIXED per-parameter cost that does not shrink with the token count of a step. Keller Jordan's own rule of thumb puts the FLOP overhead at T*d_model/tokens_per_step, which is ~0.73% at nanoGPT-speedrun scale (T=5, d=768, 524,288 tokens/step) but 62.5% here (T=5, d=128, 1,024 tokens/step) - an ~85x larger tax - so this should be the regime where the 'seconds, not steps' normalization bites hardest and possibly reverses the ranking.
question: At 0.42M params on a char LM, with the learning rate swept per optimizer so neither baseline is handicapped: (a) does Muon beat AdamW at MATCHED STEPS; (b) does it still beat AdamW at MATCHED WALL-CLOCK SECONDS on one CPU thread; (c) what is the measured per-step Newton-Schulz overhead factor, how does it scale with tokens per step, and how does it compare to the T*m/B rule; (d) how large would the overhead have to be before Muon loses?
method: nanoGPT-style char LM (2 pre-norm layers, d_model 128, 4 heads, d_ff 512, ctx 64, 419,328 params) on tiny-shakespeare, 90/10 split, 600 steps x batch 16 x ctx 64 = 614,400 tokens = 0.61 epochs. Muon is HAND-ROLLED in run.py from the algorithm description in kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon (no dependency on the reference repo, which assumes CUDA + distributed): Nesterov momentum 0.95 -> zeropower_via_newtonschulz5 with the tuned quintic (a,b,c)=(3.4445,-4.7750,2.0315), 5 iterations, spectral-norm pre-scaling -> update scaled by max(1, rows/cols)**0.5. PARAMETER SPLIT as the recipe prescribes: the eight block weight matrices (qkv 384x128, proj 128x128, fc 512x128, out 128x512, per layer; 393,216 params = 93.8%) go to Muon; token+positional embeddings, LM head and all LayerNorm gains/biases (26,112 params) stay on AdamW. FAIRNESS: lr swept per optimizer at seed 0 (AdamW [1e-3,3e-3,1e-2], Muon [1e-2,3e-2,9e-2]) with an AUTOMATIC EDGE GUARD - if the best lr lands on a grid endpoint the grid is extended one point further (x3). It fired: AdamW's best was 1e-2, the top of its grid, so 3e-2 was run too (3.554 bpc, clearly worse), leaving the AdamW optimum bracketed on both sides; Muon's optimum (3e-2) was interior from the start. In the Muon arm the auxiliary AdamW runs at AdamW's own best lr. Identical init and identical batch stream per seed across arms; identical 60-step warmup, cosine to 0.1x, grad clip 1.0, weight decay 0.01 on 2-D weights. THREE ARMS: adamw (600 steps); muon (600 steps = MATCHED STEPS); muon_isotime (470 steps = MATCHED SECONDS, where 470 = 600 / the measured in-training overhead factor and the cosine schedule is REWRITTEN over its own 470 steps, so Muon is not handicapped by a truncated LR schedule - this retrained arm, not a truncated curve reading, is the primary seconds comparison). 2 seeds at each best lr. CLOCK DISCIPLINE: every eval pass is excluded from the training wall clock; a separate INTERLEAVED A/B micro-benchmark (AdamW and Muon steps alternated within each rep, median of 6 reps) measures per-step cost at batch 8/16/32/64 so machine-load drift on this 2-shared-core box hits both arms equally. PROBES: exact Newton-Schulz FLOP count for the actual matrix shapes; a float32-vs-bfloat16 NS timing probe; per-arm optimizer-step share of wall clock. 13 runs, 547 s. SOAP DELIBERATELY SKIPPED (backlog-sanctioned): Shampoo eigenbasis + Adam needs a periodic eigendecomposition of per-layer preconditioners and does not fit the 12-minute single-thread CPU budget; the comparison is honestly renamed Muon vs AdamW in the README and in metrics.soap_included=false, and the slug is kept only so the registry lines up.
architecture: nanoGPT-style decoder-only char LM: 2 pre-norm blocks, d_model 128, 4 heads, d_ff 512 GELU MLP, learned absolute positions, ctx 64, untied 128x65 head, 419,328 params (393,216 on Muon, 26,112 on AdamW)

metrics.headline: val bpc of Muon vs AdamW at matched steps and at matched wall-clock seconds, each at its own swept-best lr, with the measured Newton-Schulz overhead factor and the break-even overhead
metrics.soap_skip_reason: SOAP (Shampoo eigenbasis + Adam) needs a periodic eigendecomposition of per-layer preconditioners; a correct implementation does not fit the 12-minute CPU budget. Backlog-sanctioned shrink; comparison honestly renamed Muon vs AdamW.

ns_precision_probe_seconds.note: seconds for ONE layer's worth of Muon matrices; x n_layer=2 for a full optimizer step

bf16_counterfactual.note: arithmetic projection from the measured precision probe, NOT a re-run: substituting the reference implementation's bfloat16 Newton-Schulz (3.4x SLOWER on this CPU) would push the overhead above the 1.8537 break-even and flip this row's verdict to 'Muon loses on wall clock' - an implementation artifact, not a property of the algorithm

result_summary: HYPOTHESIS REFUTED, IN THE INTERESTING DIRECTION. At 419,328 params on tiny-shakespeare with 1,024 tokens per step on ONE CPU THREAD - about the most hostile setting available to Muon, and the regime where Keller Jordan's own overhead rule T*d_model/tokens_per_step predicts a 62.5% tax versus 0.73% at nanoGPT-speedrun scale - Muon beats AdamW at matched STEPS by 0.3835 bpc (2.5633 vs 2.9468, both seeds same sign, 21.6x the 0.0178 mean seed spread) AND STILL beats it at matched SECONDS by 0.2738 bpc (2.6730 vs 2.9468, both seeds same sign). Both baselines are swept: an automatic lr-grid EDGE GUARD fired when AdamW's best (1e-2) landed on the top of its grid and ran 3e-2 as well (3.554 bpc, clearly worse), so the AdamW optimum is bracketed on both sides and cannot be a capped-baseline artifact; Muon's optimum (3e-2, 3x AdamW's) was interior. The matched-seconds arm is RETRAINED at 470 steps with its own cosine schedule rather than read off a truncated curve, so Muon is not handicapped by an undecayed LR; the truncated-curve reading agrees (-0.336). THE ACCOUNTING, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE ROW: the measured per-step overhead is x1.277 (+27.7%; the optimizer step goes from 7.2% of wall clock under AdamW to 33.4% under Muon, 4.3 -> 25.6 ms), while Muon's step-domain speedup is 1.85x (it reaches AdamW's final bpc in 279 steps against AdamW's 517). Muon therefore loses on wall clock only if the overhead factor exceeds the step-domain speedup - 1.277 vs 1.854, a 1.45x margin - and 1.854/1.277 = 1.45 reproduces the directly measured 1.49x wall-clock speedup, so the two accountings agree. The seconds correction is real and large - it costs Muon 29% of its per-step margin (0.383 -> 0.274 bpc) - it is simply not large enough to flip the ranking. WHY THE HYPOTHESIS FAILED: the T*m/B rule is stated as an upper bound on FLOPs and it overshoots the WALL-CLOCK cost by 2.26x here (62.5% predicted vs 47.5% by exact FLOP count for these shapes vs 27.7% measured), because the Newton-Schulz quintic is a handful of small cache-resident perfectly-shaped GEMMs that run at much higher achieved FLOP/s than a training step full of attention, GELU, embedding gathers and cross-entropy. THE FIXED-COST STRUCTURE IS CONFIRMED even though the conclusion is not: the interleaved A/B micro-benchmark gives +62.7% @512 tokens/step, +38.4% @1024, +22.6% @2048, +12.8% @4096 - a clean tokens^-0.76 decay - so the danger zone is BELOW this experiment's batch size, not above it; extrapolating the fit, break-even is only reached at ~351 tokens/step (batch 5.5 at ctx 64), i.e. on this box there is essentially no practical batch size at which the Newton-Schulz tax eats Muon's win. This extends the large-batch finding of arXiv:2505.02222 (Muon's token-ratio edge non-decreasing in batch size, 128K-16M-token batches) down 128x below their smallest batch. A CONCRETE LANDMINE, QUANTIFIED: the reference implementation runs Newton-Schulz in bfloat16, which is 3.4x SLOWER than float32 on this CPU (0.0299 vs 0.00875 s per layer's matrices); substituting it projects a Muon step of 118.7 ms and an overhead of x1.984, ABOVE the 1.854 break-even - a naive bf16 port would alone have flipped this row's verdict, as an implementation artifact rather than a property of the algorithm. CAVEATS: 600 steps at 0.61 epochs is an early-training regime where a better-conditioned optimizer has the most to gain; the AdamW bottom is flat (2.932 at 3e-3 vs 2.930 at 1e-2) so its optimum is bracketed but not finely resolved; 2 seeds; single box with 2 shared cores (mitigated by interleaved A/B timing and medians, and the headline seconds comparison is a retrained arm whose achieved budget matched to 6.8%); SOAP was skipped, so this is a two-way comparison.

novelty_check.conclusion: PARTIAL-PRIOR-ART. The comparison axis is prior art and we found its numbers. Keller Jordan's Muon post gives the algorithm, the embeddings/head-on-AdamW split, and the overhead rule 'at most T*m/B' (0.7% at nanoGPT, 0.5% at Llama-405B), and states plainly that 'Muon has a slower per-step wallclock time than AdamW'. 'Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them' (arXiv:2509.02046) is the closest methodological match - it insists on tuning every baseline and reports matrix-based optimizers at ~1.3x over a properly tuned AdamW with 'the speedup inversely proportional to model scale, decreasing from 1.4x for 0.1B to 1.1x for 1.2B' - but it deliberately compares in TOKENS, not wall clock, on the explicit grounds that 'step-wise computation overhead of matrix-based optimizers can be reduced to under 10% through proper implementation'. 'Practical Efficiency of Muon for Pretraining' (arXiv:2505.02222) states the same Theta(m/B) overhead scaling and finds Muon's token-ratio advantage non-decreasing in batch size over 128K-16M-token batches. All three measure where the rule already predicts <1% overhead, on GPU, at large batch. WHAT THIS ROW ADDS AND THE SEARCH DID NOT SURFACE: (a) the accounting run where the rule predicts 62.5% instead of 0.73% - 1 CPU thread, 1,024 tokens/step, 128x below the smallest batch in 2505.02222 - and the finding that Muon still wins; (b) a RETRAINED iso-wall-clock arm with its own cosine schedule rather than a truncated-curve reading, which is the control that makes a seconds comparison fair, reported alongside the truncated reading; (c) the measured overhead-vs-tokens/step curve (tokens^-0.76, 62.7% -> 12.8% across 8x batch) placed directly against Keller's T*m/B, showing the rule overshoots the WALL-CLOCK cost by 2.26x and quantifying the FLOP-bound-vs-achieved-FLOP/s gap; (d) the break-even framing (overhead factor 1.277 vs step-domain speedup 1.854) that states exactly when Muon loses, and the extrapolated crossover at ~351 tokens/step; (e) the measurement that the reference bfloat16 Newton-Schulz is 3.4x SLOWER on CPU and would alone have flipped the verdict; (f) an automatic lr-grid edge guard, which fired on AdamW, closing the failure mode most likely to manufacture a fake Muon win. The 'no published version of this specific accounting' claim is a negative search result over 4 web searches plus 3 direct fetches, not an exhaustive literature review; arXiv/OpenAlex APIs 403 from this environment.
